bio.en: Stewart Butterfield is a legendary founder who created Flickr and Slack (sold to Salesforce in one of tech's biggest deals), known for deep product, craft, and taste.
bio.zh: Stewart Butterfield 是一位传奇创始人，他创造了 Flickr 和 Slack（被 Salesforce 以科技圈最大交易之一收购），以深厚的产品功力、工艺与品味著称。

summary.en: Stewart shares hard-won product and leadership wisdom, including his concept of 'utility curves,' the 'owner's delusion' that makes founders overestimate their product, and the hilarious 'hyperrealistic work-like activities' he sees at companies. He discusses Parkinson's law, why craft and taste matter, and what he's learned about building things people love. The episode only scratches the surface of the wisdom locked in his head.
summary.zh: Stewart 分享了来之不易的产品与领导力智慧，包括他的“效用曲线（utility curves）”概念、让创始人高估自己产品的“所有者妄想（owner's delusion）”，以及他在公司里观察到的滑稽的“超现实工作式活动（hyperrealistic work-like activities）”。他讨论了帕金森定律、为什么工艺与品味重要，以及他在打造受人喜爱之物中学到的东西。本期仅仅触及了他脑海中封存智慧的冰山一角。

I said, "I feel like what we have right now is just a giant piece of shit. It's just terrible and we should be humiliated that we offer this to the public." (00:00:14): To me that was like, "You should be embarrassed." If you can't see almost limitless opportunities to improve, then you shouldn't be designing the product.
turns.zh: 2014年。这一年，Slack正式上线。我接受《麻省理工科技评论》采访时，被问及是否在努力改进Slack。我回答：“我觉得我们现在做的东西简直就是一堆垃圾。太糟糕了，我们把这种产品推向公众，简直应该感到羞耻。”（00:00:14）对我来说，这句话就像是在说：“你应该感到丢脸。”如果你看不到几乎无限的改进机会，那你就不该去设计产品。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: At more than one company all hands, I made everyone in the company repeat this as a chant. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You started two companies, both famously pivoted. I imagine many people come to you for advice on pivoting.

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To prep for this chat, I talked to so many people that have worked with you over the years to try to figure out what you taught them about building product, building teams, building companies that most stuck with them, that most helped them build amazing products. The first is a concept called utility curves. This came up a bunch across so many people that have worked with you. Talk about what is a utility curve, how you use that to build better products.
turns.zh: 为了准备这次对谈，我和许多曾与您共事过的人聊天，试图找出您教给他们最多、最有助于他们打造优质产品、组建团队、创办公司的理念。第一个是"效用曲线"这个概念。在许多与您共事过的人那里，这个概念都被反复提及。您能解释一下什么是效用曲线，以及如何利用它来打造更好的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: This is pretty easy because it's a very familiar S-curve where you have, it's flat and it starts arcing up and then there's a really steep part and then it levels off again. And on the horizontal axis, you can think of cost or effort and on the vertical axis, it's value or convenience. It depends exactly what you're talking about, but the idea is the first bit of effort you put into something doesn't result in a huge amount of value. And then there's some magic threshold where it produces an enormous amount of value and then continued investment doesn't really pay off. The most basic example I can think of is let's say you're making a hammer, and on that bottom axis, it's now quality, and if the hammer has a handle that breaks with any impact, then is totally useless. And if you make it a little bit stronger, it's still pretty useless and it's like junk, junk, junk, junk, junk. Okay, good, great. Then it doesn't matter anymore. (00:08:06): If you're making an app, okay, this app's going to have users and so let's make a user's table and a database, and so far you have generated no value. The reason I felt like this was so important is because we would talk about a feature, and usually features are thought of as a binary. You either have this feature or you don't. The argument I guess was have we just not invested enough in this or have we got all the value or convenience or quality or whatever that we could get out of this? And we had pointed diminishing returns and it just doesn't matter. (00:08:46): I think in many cases, people will add a feature, it's not good enough and so people don't use it or appreciate it, but now you've added some complexity to the app and then people give up or take it back or they try something in testing and they don't get the results they want, and so they decide that this a thing is worth doing. We would try to really investigate and decide whether we were on the first shallow part of the curve, the second shallow part of the curve, or we're just coming up to it. So I think it's a lot easier to understand the value of this when you're talking about a specific app and a specific feature, but I think it was ultimately helpful in getting people to understand whether something was worth it or not.
turns.zh: 这其实挺容易理解的，因为这是一个非常常见的S曲线：起初是平缓的，然后开始逐渐上升，接着会出现一个陡峭的阶段，之后又会趋于平缓。在横轴上，可以理解为成本或投入；在纵轴上，则是价值或便利性。这取决于你具体讨论的内容，但核心思想是，你最初投入的努力并不会立即产生巨大的价值。然后会达到一个神奇的临界点，在此点上价值会激增，而后续的投入就无法获得更多回报。最基本的例子是，比如你要制作一把锤子，在纵轴上衡量的是质量。如果锤子的手柄一受冲击就断裂，那它就完全没用了。而如果你把手柄做得稍微结实一点，用户体验还是很差，简直就是垃圾、垃圾、垃圾、垃圾、垃圾。好的，很好。这就对了。（00:08:06）：如果是开发应用程序，首先要创建用户表和数据库，此时还没有创造任何价值。我觉得这个概念很重要，因为我们通常会把功能视为二元对立的——要么有这个功能，要么没有。争论的焦点在于，是我们投入不够，还是已经榨干了这个功能的所有价值、便利性或质量？而当我们遇到收益递减时，就无需再纠结了。（00:08:46）：很多时候，人们添加一个功能，但用户反馈不佳，于是放弃使用。但这时应用的复杂度增加了，用户又会退缩，或者在测试中尝试新功能却达不到预期效果，最终认定这个功能不值得投入。我们会仔细分析，判断当前处于曲线的哪个阶段——是平缓的初期阶段，还是即将攀升的阶段。因此，具体到某个应用和特定功能时，理解其价值会更容易。但这个框架最终有助于让人们明白某项投入是否值得。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield

And again, this axis can be, utility is the best general term for it, but it could be quality, convenience, speed, it could be any number of things, but as you improve your search capability or as you improve your login experience or your forget password experience or your checkout experience or whatever everyone else is as well. (00:11:22): I want to give an example at the absolute extreme because I actually don't know how long this has been, but I try not to criticize other people's software so much because I'm very familiar with the trade-offs and prioritization and how hard it can be and blah, blah, blah, blah. And then you're like, "Well, fuck, I can't remember which one is Daylight Savings and which one is standard time?" I could keep going like this for a while. There's so many, there's all these clever things you could do. Like you know me, I'm on the West Coast, first option should be the East Coast and vice versa. But it definitely shouldn't be that every time zone is presented with equal value. I don't a couple hundred time zones. I grew up in Canada. Newfoundland has its own time zone, which is offset by half an hour. The population of Newfoundland has about half a million people. Not that many people go to visit Newfoundland, maybe a million people in all of history so like a million and a half out of 8 billion people. And there's Newfoundland, the same with China time, which is like 25% of the world's population in this. (00:13:51): Anyway, that was a little bit longer than I intended to go on this example, but it's crazy because no one's going to switch to Gmail or to G Suite, Google Calendar from Outlook Exchange because the time zone picker is good, so maybe in some sense it doesn't matter, but at the same time there's a real value in delighting customers and there's an emotional connection that they form or don't form. And in some cases that could be really positive like they would recommend it. And when they switch companies or decide to start their own company, they're going to choose to use this product or advocate for it because of that emotional connection and vice versa. (00:14:34): They'll also be like, "I hate this thing that drives me bananas. I really think we should stop using it," or advocate for the alternative. And I think people just don't appreciate or come back to those things often enough. And then there's this category of really essential parts of the app again like account creation, sign up, forgot password, things like that, that for most organizations very infrequently get a lot of love and iteration and improvement despite the fact that the quality bar has gone up across the board and continually goes up.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得你还需要引入另一个概念，比如贝索斯提到的"神圣的不满"。用户需求其实会不断升级，因为一旦人们熟悉了一款软件或某项功能的实现方式，他们的标准就会提高，从而引发竞争。可以把这看作一个维度——实用性是最通用的衡量标准，但也可以是质量、便利性、速度等任何指标。当你提升搜索功能、优化登录体验、改进忘记密码流程或结账流程时，其他平台也在同步改进。因此需要持续投入精力——别光想着新功能，更多要关注产品的整体体验。大多数功能一次性实现后，如果幸运的话会定期优化，但很多功能根本从未改进过。

（00:11:22）：我要举个极端例子，因为我不太想批评别人的软件，毕竟我深知其中的权衡、优先级排序和挑战。但好吧，大多数人手机上都有Gmail日历应用。我经常出差，主要在东部时区，有时转换到山地时区、太平洋时区或英国时间、日本时间，总共可能涉及10个甚至12个时区。当你在iOS应用中设置日历事件的时区时，它按字母顺序列出全球所有时区。虽然可能有更合理的排序，但这个排序毫无价值。

（00:12:24）：即使你开始搜索时，它还是按国家字母顺序排列。比如我在加州，计划下周回纽约时预约会议，输入"E-A-S-T"却得到一堆乱码——东部时间，首先是澳大利亚东部，然后是新南威尔士州，再是昆士兰州，最后是夏令时和标准时。接着你会想："妈的，记不清哪个是夏令时，哪个是标准时了？"我可以继续列举下去。这款应用至少有数亿用户，估计每个谷歌员工都用过。如此糟糕的体验简直离谱。本地化处理本可以有很多巧思。比如我住在西海岸，首选选项应该优先东海岸，反之亦然。但每个时区都被平等对待实在不可理喻。我不关心几百个时区，我在加拿大长大，纽芬兰有自己的时区，偏差半小时。纽芬兰人口约50万，历史上可能只有100万游客去过，总数不过80亿分之1500万。中国时区也是如此，覆盖全球25%人口。

（00:13:51）：总之，举这个例子比我预期的要长，但问题在于没人会因为Gmail或G Suite的时区选择器好用而从Outlook Exchange切换到Gmail。所以从某种意义上说这无关紧要，但同时为客户创造愉悦体验确实有价值。
他们之间会形成或不形成某种情感联结。在某些情况下，这种联结可能是非常积极的，比如他们会向他人推荐这款产品。当他们跳槽到其他公司，或者决定自己创业时，他们会因为这种情感联结而选择继续使用这款产品，或者为其发声，反之亦然。（00:14:34）他们也会说：“我讨厌这个让我抓狂的东西，我真的觉得我们应该停用它。”或者力荐替代方案。我觉得人们往往没有充分重视这些功能，或者不常回顾它们。再比如应用中的基础模块，比如账户创建、注册、忘记密码之类的，尽管整体质量标准在不断提高，但对于大多数组织而言，这些模块很少得到足够的关注、迭代和改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's go down that rabbit hole a little bit more around delight and craft. Slack was famous for being one of the early, let's say consumerized B2B SaaS products. Slack leaned into delight and experience and craft and a great experience. And you just as a product leader, I'd say are known as very taste forward, very craft oriented leader, which is pretty rare and I think continues to be rare. So there's a few things I want to talk about here. One is taste. I heard at a talk, you gave a talk on taste and you have a really unique perspective on just what taste is, what product taste looks like. Can you share that?
turns.zh: 让我们再深入探讨一下“愉悦感”和“精巧设计”这两个主题。Slack曾以其早期面向消费者的B2B SaaS产品而闻名。该公司致力于打造令人愉悦的用户体验，注重产品设计的精巧性。而作为产品负责人，您被公认为一位极具审美眼光、注重设计细节的领导者——这种特质实属难得，且至今仍属凤毛麟角。接下来我想谈谈几个关键点：首先是"审美"。我曾听过您的一场演讲，您在其中深入探讨了审美理念，并对产品审美特质提出了独到见解。您能否与我们分享您的见解？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: There is a lot of you going back to the utility curves again, people who are obsessed with this one little thing and keep on adding more and more detailed improvements beyond the point where it makes much of a difference. But I guess a couple of things about taste. So one is can you learn to develop it? I think so because the word literally comes from experiencing food and putting stuff in your mouth. And can people become better chefs with training? Yes, absolutely. Undoubtedly, some people have a natural advantage and are born with this ability to make discernments that are difficult for other people to make and stuff like that. But you can definitely practice and you can definitely get better. The second thing I'd say is you can create a real advantage for yourself, for your product, for your company by leaning into it because most people don't have good taste and don't invest. You're probably familiar with, again, Jeff Bezos line, your margin is my opportunity and pretty obvious what he meant by that. (00:16:54): I would tell the story at Slack over and over again. It actually made it part of the new hire welcome. I'm in Vancouver at our Vancouver office and I'm going for a walk with Brandon Velestuk who's our, at the time creative director for product development, I think that was his title. And we're in the Yaletown neighborhood in Vancouver so there's really narrow sidewalks because it used to be a warehouse district and now it's fancy restaurants and nail salons and boutiques and stuff. And as it does in Vancouver, it starts to rain. We don't have umbrellas. We're walking back to the office and most people have umbrellas and we're on these narrow sidewalks with people coming towards us with umbrellas. We noticed how few people would move their umbrella out of the way. And of course, the other person, their umbrella, the pokey bits are exactly at eye level for people walking towards them. We would get forced off the sidewalk or having to duck down or whatever. (00:17:54): It became a game like we were guessing is this person going to tilt their umbrella out of the way so we can pass or not? And something like one-third of the people would do it. And we had this conversation about it where it's like, okay, I can think of three reasons why people wouldn't do it. One is they have very few avenues in their life to exercise power and this is one of them. And they're just, want to get out there and dominate people and cause suffering. Shouldn't ascribe to malice that which can be ascribed to ignorance so that probably is the explanation for a tiny, tiny, tiny percentage of people. (00:18:34): But the other two explanations aren't that great either. One is that they see it's happening, they see they're pushing other people off the sidewalk or poking them in the eye or whatever, and they're just like, "Fuck, that's too bad. I wish there was something I could do about that, but I can't think of anything." And the last reason is they just don't notice it all. They're just oblivious to their impact on other people. And they're so in their head, and I can't really think of any other explanations for it besides that. (00:19:03): And so we would say it's not like tilting your umbrella is our opportunity. That's not a great rephrase of your margin is my opportunity, but your failure to really be consider it exercise this courtesy and really be empathic about other people's experience is an advantage that you can create a critical advantage. I think that there's many reasons why Slack was successful at the moment. It was successful and we think we had a bunch of really wonderful tailwinds and all of that stuff, but it wouldn't have grown the way it did without those little conveniences which caused people to form an emotional connection because a lot of our growth came from startup A uses Slack, and then someone leaves startup A for startup B, and startup B doesn't use Slack yet. And they would be like, "Oh my God, you guys, you really, this is so good. We got to try it." And the spread was driven by that and people really genuinely advocating for it.
turns.zh:
很多人又回到了效用曲线那套思维，沉迷于某个细节，不断添加越来越多的改进，直到这些改进已经无法带来实质性提升。但我觉得这其中有几个关于审美的问题。首先，你能否学会培养这种审美能力？我认为可以，因为审美本质上源于品尝食物、将食物放入口中体验的过程。通过训练，人能成为更好的厨师吗？当然可以。毫无疑问，有些人天生就具有敏锐的判断力，能分辨出别人难以察觉的细微差别。但通过刻意练习，你一定能提升自己的审美水平。

其次，你可以为自己、产品或公司创造真正的竞争优势。大多数人审美欠佳且不愿投入精力，而你可以利用这一点。（00:16:54）我曾在Slack反复讲过这个故事。它甚至成为新员工入职培训的核心内容。我在温哥华的办公室，与时任产品开发创意总监的布兰登·维莱斯图克（Brandon Velestuk）散步。当时我们身处耶鲁镇（Yaletown），这片曾是仓库区的街区，如今遍布高档餐厅、美甲沙龙和精品店。我们散步时，雨突然下起来。我们没带伞，而大多数人都有伞。狭窄的人行道上，迎面走来的行人往往不愿为我们让路。

（00:17:54）这场游戏变得有趣起来——我们猜测对方会不会把伞移开，让我们通过。结果只有约三分之一的人会这么做。我们讨论了原因：第一，他们在生活中鲜有行使权力的机会，而雨中让路就是一个机会；第二，他们可能想压制他人或制造困扰。当然，不能把恶意归因于无知，所以这只适用于极少数人。（00:18:34）其余两种解释也不乐观：一种是他们明明看到自己推搡他人或挡住视线，却无动于衷；另一种是他们完全忽视了自己的影响。总之，审美能力的提升需要刻意培养，而非被动接受。

（00:19:03）所以我们说，雨伞的倾斜不是商机，但不为他人着想的冷漠，却能转化为竞争优势。Slack的成功绝非偶然，关键在于
尽管我们确实得益于诸多有利因素，但若没有那些让用户产生情感共鸣的小功能，业务增长绝不会如此显著。比如，我们的很多用户都是从初创公司A转战到初创公司B的，而B公司当时尚未启用Slack平台。用户们会惊呼：“天哪，兄弟们，这东西真是太棒了，我们必须试试看！” 正是这种口口相传的推荐，推动了Slack的广泛普及，也让用户们真心实意地为它站台宣传。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing metaphor. I love that one moment became a value of product craftsmanship at Slack.
turns.zh: 这真是个绝妙的比喻。我很欣赏Slack将某个瞬间升华为产品工艺价值的做法。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Tilt your umbrella was a very common saying on company swag and stuff like that.
turns.zh: "把伞倒过"曾是公司周边商品上常见的俏皮说法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example, I imagine there are many, but from the time of building Slack, especially in the early days where you chose to go big on craftsmanship and experience and delight versus speed where you thought looking back that was a really great idea and worth really core just to success.
turns.zh: 有没有相关例子？我相信有很多案例，但回顾Slack的发展历程，尤其是在早期阶段，我们选择在工艺、体验和愉悦感上投入重注，而非追求速度。现在看来，这确实是个明智的决策，对公司的成功至关重要。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Here's a bunch of little examples. Someone else came up with this idea, and I'm trying to remember who it was, but let's see, maybe Andrea Torres, maybe Ben Brown, something like that who was like, "Why did we ask people for email address and password if their ownership of the email address was the thing that allowed them to create the account in the first place? Why don't we just ask them for their email address and then send them a link?" (00:21:07): And so when Slack's first version of the mobile app came out, we're like, "Typing your password on your phone if you have any minimal threshold of password hygiene is a terrible experience." Capital H, lowercase Q, six, caret, period. So let's just have them enter the email address. We'll send them a link. The link will automatically open the app and authenticate them. And so there's one, a little example.
turns.zh: 这里有几个小例子。有人曾提出这样的想法，我记不清具体是谁了，可能是安德烈娅·托雷斯或本·布朗之类的人，他们问道："如果用户拥有邮箱地址本身就能创建账户，为什么还要让他们输入邮箱和密码呢？我们为什么不直接让用户输入邮箱，然后发送一个链接呢？"（00:21:07）当Slack的首款移动应用上线时，我们发现："在手机上输入密码，尤其是对于那些有基本密码卫生意识的人来说，体验太糟糕了。"大写的H，小写的Q，数字6，符号^，句号。于是我们决定让用户直接输入邮箱地址，发送链接后，链接会自动打开应用并完成认证。这就是其中一个小例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So you guys invented the magic link experience.
turns.zh: 哇。所以你们发明了魔法链接体验。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Someone else invented. I want to be clear that I had seen that idea somewhere else, someone else, a blog post about it or something like that. But we were the first ones, to my knowledge, that really scaled that and made it a standard. There is another one which we really puzzled about in the very early days where people have a long history of using messaging apps from AOL Instant Messenger to SMS to WhatsApp, where their expectation is they get a notification for every message that's received. And in the case of Slack, that doesn't make as much sense because you're a member of many channels and the messages may not be for you, and so that's why we have the @ tagging people. And we certainly didn't invent that, that was Twitter. (00:22:23): But what we realized was people were signing up for Slack, and it's one engineer on this team inside of this larger organization, inside this larger company, and they would pull in the person next to them and they would say, "Let's try it out." (00:22:35): And then they would send a message and then one person would be like, "I didn't get a notification. This is bullshit." (00:22:43): We reluctantly decided that we had to send notifications for every single message as the default for new accounts. But once you had, I don't remember what the threshold would happen, I think it's once you had received 10 messages, we would pop up this little thing that says, "Hey, you have our default settings for notifications. We don't want Slack to be noisy for you. Would you like to switch to our-"
turns.zh: 其实是别人先发明的。我要说明的是，我在其他地方见过这个想法，比如某个博客文章之类的。但据我所知，我们是首家将其大规模推广并使其成为标准的公司。还有一个例子，在Slack早期阶段，我们对用户长期使用的消息应用（从AOL Instant Messenger到短信再到WhatsApp）深有体会——用户期望每条收到的消息都能收到通知。但在Slack的场景下，这就说不通了，因为用户可能加入多个频道，而这些消息并非都针对他们。因此我们引入了@标签功能。虽然这并非Slack首创（Twitter早有此功能），但我们意识到用户注册Slack后，团队中的某位工程师会拉来旁边的人试用，然后发送消息后，对方会抱怨"没收到通知，这太糟糕了"。最终我们无奈地决定，默认新用户账户会收到每条消息的通知。但当用户收到10条消息后，系统会弹出提示："您当前使用的是我们的默认通知设置。我们不想让Slack成为您的信息轰炸机。您是否想切换到我们的……"

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: ... For notifications. We don't want Slack to be noisy for you. Would you like to switch to our recommended settings? And then they would just click a link and it would have what should be the default, which is, you only get a notification if it's a DM or someone tags you. But we realized it was worth that investment to get people over the hump. I'll give one more simple one and then one kind of more complex. One, people would just like the, I can't remember if it's called urgent or important, but the flag in Outlook, set the priority of a message for the recipients always got abused inside of every company. As soon as someone does it, everyone's like, "Okay, I'm going to do that too for my message." (00:23:41): And so all of your messages have the little flag and it becomes useless. We have @everyone, which causes a notification to be sent to every member of the channel when the message is sent and people would start, someone would find this feature inside of a organization. They would @everyone, everyone would get a notification and then the next person to send a message who was like, " Well, my thing's more important than Bob's thing. I'm going to also @everyone." And it became really obnoxious and people would complain about it, but it was, I don't know, I guess tragedy of the commons. It's not quite exactly the same thing, but it was this real dynamic that happened over and over again. (00:24:16): So we came up with what was called the shouty rooster, and internally we said, "Don't be a cock." But we didn't obviously say that publicly when you @everyone, a little rooster would pop up and it would have you sound waves coming out of its mouth and being really obnoxious and say, "Hey, this is going to cause a notification for 147 people in eight different time zones. Are you sure you want to send this message with the @everyone?" And of course, that worked amazingly and it dropped off. And again, it was really trying to shape people's behavior so that they used, one is not to be very flexible, but we knew that there was ways to use it that would be annoying and difficult for everyone. And so try to shape the communication culture inside the organization to take best advantage on it.
turns.zh: 关于通知功能。我们不想让Slack变得过于烦人。您是否愿意切换到我们推荐的设置？然后，用户只需点击一个链接，就能看到默认设置——只有收到直接消息或被他人@时，才会收到通知。但我们意识到，投入这项功能是值得的，能帮助用户适应新规则。我再举个简单例子，还有个更复杂的案例。首先，Outlook中的“紧急”或“重要”标记功能常被滥用。只要有人启用这个功能，所有人都想效仿，结果所有邮件都被打上小旗标记，失去了实际意义。我们推出了@全员功能，发送消息时会向频道所有成员发送通知。但有些人发现这个功能后，会@全员，导致所有人收到通知，随后又有其他人@全员，形成恶性循环，用户纷纷抱怨。但这就是所谓的公共资源悲剧，虽然不完全相同，但这种动态反复上演。于是我们设计了提示语：“别当老大哥。”当用户@全员时，会弹出一只生气的小公鸡，嘴里发出刺耳的提示音：“嘿，这条消息会通知8个时区的147人。你确定要发送吗？”结果效果显著，滥用行为减少了。我们致力于规范用户行为，既不限制灵活性，又避免了不必要的麻烦，最终让沟通文化更高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That feature still exists. I see that rooster all the, no, I don't see it all, well, actually I do @channel, because I run a big Slack, so I see that rooster, that survived.
turns.zh: 这个功能至今还在用。我到处都能看到那个小公鸡，不，不全能看到，实际上我用@频道功能，因为我管理着一个大Slack频道，所以能看到那个公鸡，它至今还在用。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, that survived and good because it was a trivially easy thing to implement and made a really big difference. But it also taught people how the product worked, because people probably didn't know that @everyone or @channel... Didn't think about the cost, at least.
turns.zh: 是啊。这功能确实保留下来了，挺好的，因为实现起来简单，却带来了巨大改变。它还让用户了解了产品的运作机制，可能之前很多人都不知道@全员或@频道的后果……至少他们没考虑过成本问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Genius.
turns.zh: 真是高明。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. Here's one more. So we decided we were going to Do Not Disturb as a feature. And we had this, not conundrum, but you're trying to take into account all the different uses of Slack because by the time we implemented this, 2017, there was tens of thousands of paying customers, the organizations, hundreds of probably millions of users, maybe hundreds of thousands of organizations. I don't remember how many. And everyone had set up stuff the way that they liked it, including things like ops alerts going into channels for on-call engineers for some of the biggest systems and apps in the world. And so we couldn't just deploy it right away. We realized that some of the decision-makers, the owners of the organizations were going to have really strong opinions about this. We also realized that some of the end users are going to have strong opinions, and we wanted to figure out a way to balance the concerns and give people appropriate means of control. (00:26:37): So we came up with this really elaborate system for the rollout, which was, we told everyone, I'm sorry, every Slack administrator that this was coming weeks before it came. And we told them that we were going to set a default for their organization, which I believe was either 7:00 P.M. to 7:00 A.M. in their local time zone, or 8: 00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M., I can't remember which it was, but also that they could override that default, and also that the individual end users could override that system owner default. And finally, that the system owner could, if they changed the default again, would override all of the end user's preferences and then the end users could override them again. And it wasn't to create this dynamic where people were at war, but so that you could change a policy and then people could still customize and stuff like that. (00:27:32): But this was a much longer and more convoluted process, but it allowed the millions of people who were using Slack to get the feature without creating a bunch of conflict and without people turning it off automatically. And I think critically, with setting a bunch of defaults, because if we didn't set the default, most people wouldn't turn it on at all. If we didn't default you to Do Not Disturb from 8:00 P.M. to 8:00 A.M. you probably, if you're the average person, wouldn't ever do it yourself. So that's another elaborate example where I think that investment made sense because it was a critical feature for a lot of people. And if we hadn't done it that way, I think it would've caused a lot of complaints and conflict and stuff like that.

是的。再讲一个例子。我们决定将“免打扰”功能纳入产品设计。说实话，这并非难题，但我们需要兼顾Slack的多种使用场景。2017年我们上线这项功能时，Slack已拥有数万名付费客户和数百家企业，用户规模更是达数百万，企业数量可能有数千家——具体数字我记不清了。每个用户都按照自己的习惯设置了各种功能，比如为全球大型系统和应用的值班工程师开通的紧急通知通道等。因此，我们不能一股脑地直接上线这项功能。我们意识到，部分决策者和企业主对此会有强烈意见，终端用户同样会有强烈反响。我们需要找到平衡各方利益的方案，赋予用户适当的控制权。  
（00:26:37）：为此，我们设计了一个精心策划的上线流程。我们提前数周告知所有Slack管理员即将推出该功能，并承诺会为他们的组织设定默认时间段——我记得当时是本地时区的晚上7点至次日早上7点，或者上午8点至晚上8点，具体记不清了。但用户可以覆盖默认设置，系统管理员也可以重新调整默认值，同时终端用户也可以覆盖系统管理员的默认设置。最后，系统管理员再次更改默认值时，所有用户偏好都会被覆盖，用户又可以重新调整。我们的目标不是制造冲突，而是让政策调整后的用户仍能保持个性化设置。  
（00:27:32）：这个过程漫长而复杂，但它让数百万Slack用户顺利获得了这项功能，避免了大规模冲突和用户主动关闭该功能的情况。关键在于设置默认值——如果不默认启用，多数用户根本不会主动开启。例如，如果不将默认时间段设为晚上8点至次日早上8点，普通用户很可能永远不会自己启用该功能。这就是一个成功的例子，说明为何这项对许多人至关重要的功能值得投入精力打造。如果当初没有这样做，必将引发大量抱怨和冲突。

turns.zh: 我还听说你们经常提倡的一点是，产品体验中的摩擦感对很多人来说是反直觉的。但很多时候，合理利用这种摩擦感反而是件好事。如果处理得当，它就是一项功能而非漏洞。能否谈谈你们在这方面的经验？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. So yes, and there's also another issue around friction, which is it became like a mantra or just kind of an assumption that you should always be trying to remove friction. And in some cases that's true. We would talk about it in Slack. It was hard to market. It was hard to explain what it was if you had never used it before. You could say a messaging app for businesses or whatever, but a critical disadvantage to Slack doing out-of-home advertising, putting up a billboard versus beer or cars is, no one needs to be explained why they would want a car or beer, but everyone will have to explain one day why they want Slack. And so the problem there is comprehension, and this will come up an enormous amount. So now imagine you want to get tickets to the Taylor Swift concert in San Francisco and you go to the Ticketmaster website. (00:29:43): If you think about both your comprehension, it's perfect to this case. And that translates into the specificity of your intent and the degree of your intent is also kind of maxed out. So look, I really want to get these tickets. I know exactly what they are. They're Taylor Swift tickets for this date at this venue. And so in that scenario, it doesn't really matter if Ticketmaster's website is slow, it doesn't really matter if the payments page errors out, you're going to persist and get through it. So obviously they're better to reduce friction, but in some sense there's not a huge amount of value in doing that. For most creators of products, there are a handful of cases where that really is true for you as well. And they include things like user registration, authentication, checkout flows for e-commerce. I am significantly more likely to buy something if there's Apple Pay or Shop Pay or something like that. (00:30:44): I'm significantly less likely to carry through the purchase of something if I have to manually enter all of the fields of my address one at a time rather than having one of those address pickers. It's crazy, but the issue is my intent isn't always 100%, and the specificity of my intent isn't always 100%. So if your thing is direct to consumer T-shirts and you acquire customers through Instagram ads, all of them know what T-shirts are. It's like, "This looks like a good T-shirt to me." But I'm rarely 100% intent. I might have a very specific intent, but my intent's like 70%. So if you're, the amount of friction is above that, I'm not going to do it. But now, okay, people coming to Slack.com, some friend had mentioned Slack and talked their ear off at some point months ago, and then they saw a news article and then they saw someone's tweet and then they saw an ad on about the website they were visiting and they finally said, "Okay, I'm going to go to this website." (00:31:46): So their intent is at the absolute minimum threshold, it was before that last event happened, they were below and now they're above, but they're just above. The specificity of their intent like, "I need to get Taylor Swift concerts for this date at this venue." Is also very low, because they're like, "It's a work thing. I'm not sure it's a spreadsheet or a calendar or exactly what it is." So they were coming in at 0.1% over these critical thresholds. What was the challenge? It wasn't friction, because it's not like they were aiming for something and they knew what they were aiming for and they were just trying to get themselves to that point. (00:32:34): What we had to worry about was creating comprehension and in two senses, what is this thing? And what am I supposed to do next? And that creation of comprehension in the sense of explaining stuff, that creation of comprehension in the sense of the design of the UI, of the screen, of the page or whatever, and the visual hierarchy and the affordances that are there and the indication of things to interact with and which thing should be the next thing to do and all that stuff, that becomes really critical. (00:33:09): And I think very, very few people recognize that. They're like, "I want to get people who come to my webpage to the sign up form as quickly as possible." But if they don't know what they're signing up for and they don't know what it's going to do after, is it going to spam them? They don't know, "Am I going to have to pay on the next step or what?" Then they're just going to back out. And this was a lifelong battle because the remove friction orientation is so deep in people. Again, it really makes a difference in those cases where people do have an intent and they do know what they're trying to do is a poor approach when the challenge is really comprehension, and I think the secret is most, 70%, 80% or whatever of a product design is in that comprehension step because people, if they do ever open the preferences tab and look at all the options, rarely have an idea. (00:34:09): And if you can't teach them or make it possible for them to discover what the capabilities are, then they're not going to take advantage of them and they're not going to get as much out of it. And I think that the trick is for most of the unique parts of any application, most of the specific things that your app, your product, your software does are areas where the challenge is going to be comprehension inside of friction. It really could be anything Shopify, the purpose of the service for its end users is generally going to be kind to clear. But most people, most first-time store openers don't know that they can get reports or if they know that they can get reports, they don't know what kinds of reports. And if they know what kinds of reports they can get, they don't know how they can tweak them and what the timing should be and which things that are more important to display. (00:35:03): And I could go on and on and on and on, and people just don't recognize that. So I want to see if this is still true. I'm just going to open my phone and clock app. And they had the craziest description for alarms. It's a little bit different, but people can look at their own phone. So I have, it says alarms and it says sleep and a vertical bar, wake up and says, no alarm, and a button that says change. And then if you hit it, it says sleep is off. In order to automatically turn on sleep features and edit your schedule, you need to turn sleep on. So obviously sleep was a good name for this thing if you already had a way of getting people to understand it. If you don't, it's ungrammatical and incomprehensible and why would you ever do it? And I got to guess, it's been like this for years, 90 plus percent and maybe 98% of people just do what I do, which is that you just create, "I want the alarm on and I'm going to set the time for it." (00:36:11): And I don't know what turning sleep on does, but it's just the lack of comprehension prevents people from getting the value. And I'm sure that there's a bunch of value behind turning sleep on, whatever that means and people spend a lot of time on those features and it integrates with biometrics and your watch or who knows. Again, I still don't know because turning sleep on is like, what does that do? And what is it going to cost me? And what impact it's going to have? Those examples are just to me all over the place. And the reason I don't use most software where there was an actual choice point or the reason I don't use most features where there was a choice point for me is because I didn't understand what they were going to do and I don't give a shit. And if there is one mantra that I would use to replace that it's, Don't Make Me Think, I don't know if you remember that book.

是啊。所以没错，还有一个关于降低摩擦成本的问题。人们总把“减少摩擦”当作口头禅，或者认为理所当然地认为你应该一直努力消除摩擦。在某些情况下，这确实没错。我们在Slack上讨论过这个问题。推广Slack的难度很大。对于从未使用过该应用的人，要解释清楚它的功能很困难。你可以说它是面向企业的消息应用之类的，但Slack在户外广告（比如广告牌宣传）方面的劣势在于——没人需要解释为什么要买车或啤酒，但每个人都得解释为什么要用Slack。关键问题在于理解成本，这在未来会成为一个巨大的挑战。想象你想买Taylor Swift在旧金山的演唱会门票，登录Ticketmaster网站。（00:29:43）：从理解成本的角度来看，这个例子很典型。你的需求非常明确，意图也极其清晰。所以你会坚持不懈地完成购买。即使Ticketmaster网站速度慢，支付页面出错，也不会阻止你达成目标。因此，降低摩擦成本固然重要，但在某些情况下其价值并不显著。对于大多数产品开发者来说，有几个场景确实如此，比如用户注册、身份验证、电商结账流程等。如果有Apple Pay或Shop Pay等支付方式，我更有可能购买商品。（00:30:44）：如果必须手动逐个输入地址信息，而不是使用地址选择器，我购买意愿会大打折扣。这听起来很疯狂，但问题在于用户的意图并不总是百分之百明确，具体需求也不总是清晰。比如直接面向消费者的T恤销售，通过Instagram广告获客的人都知道T恤是什么。“这件T恤看起来不错。”但他们的意图往往不达标。可能有明确的需求，但意图程度只有70%。如果摩擦成本超过这个门槛，他们就不会购买。再看Slack的案例。有人几个月前在Instagram上大力推荐Slack，用户看到新闻报道和推特推荐，最后才访问Slack官网。（00:31:46）：他们的意图在最初低于关键门槛，后来才勉强达标，但仍处于边缘状态。具体需求同样模糊，比如“我需要购买Taylor Swift旧金山演唱会门票”，但用户可能只是出于工作需要，不确定具体用途。所以他们的意图评分只有0.1%。挑战不在于摩擦成本，因为用户目标明确，只是需要引导他们完成购买。（00:32:34）：我们需要关注两个方面：用户理解和下一步操作指引。比如“这是什么东西？”和“接下来该做什么？”
理解的含义在于解释事物——无论是用户界面设计、屏幕布局、页面结构，还是视觉层次与交互提示，比如提示用户接下来该做什么之类的。这些元素都至关重要。（00:33:09）：但我发现很少有人意识到这一点。他们只想着“让访问者尽快完成注册流程”。但如果用户不清楚注册后的用途，不知道后续流程会怎样（比如是否会被狂轰滥炸的邮件骚扰），甚至不确定下一步是否需要付费，他们就会退出。这是一场持久战，因为“消除摩擦”的思维定式根深蒂固。实际上，当用户有明确需求但不了解操作流程时，传统方法反而适得其反。产品设计的70%、80%甚至更多精力都应投入到理解环节，因为即便用户打开偏好设置选项卡查看所有选项，多数人也摸不着头脑。（00:34:09）：如果无法教会用户或让他们自行探索功能，他们就无法充分利用产品。Shopify这类应用的大部分独特功能，多数用户根本不了解其核心价值。例如，用户可能不知道如何获取报表，即便知道报表功能，也不清楚如何调整参数、设置提醒时机或优先显示哪些数据。（00:35:03）：类似例子不胜枚举，但人们往往忽视这一点。让我验证一下这个观点。打开手机的闹钟应用，他们对闹钟功能的描述堪称离谱。应用标题写着“闹钟”和“睡眠”，还配有竖线分隔符，标注“关闭闹钟”和“更改设置”。点击“更改”，系统提示“睡眠功能已关闭”。要自动开启睡眠功能并编辑日程，必须先开启睡眠模式。显然，如果用户已有对应理解路径，取名“睡眠”是合理的。但若缺乏引导，用户只能被动操作，完全摸不着头脑。想必多年来90%以上用户都和我一样：直接设置闹钟时间，却忽略睡眠功能的深层价值。（00:36:11）：我至今仍不明白开启睡眠功能的具体作用，成本与收益也未明朗。或许它与生物识别数据、手表同步等功能深度整合，但我仍困惑于其逻辑：开启睡眠功能究竟有何用？会产生哪些影响？
那些例子对我来说简直乱成一团。之所以我不使用大多数有明确选择项的软件，或者不使用那些有选择项但我根本不明白其用途的功能，原因很简单——我压根儿不明白它们能做什么，而且我根本不在乎。如果要用一句口头禅来替代这个理念，那就是“别让我思考”（Don't Make Me Think），不知道你们是否还记得这本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对是这样。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. And honestly, it's been many more than 10 years since I read it, so I don't even remember all of the examples in the book, but as a mantra that was up there with utility curves because for two reasons. One is it's just like it's expensive to make a decision. You literally burn glucose. There's a metabolic action. There's ATP created in the mitochondria and your neurons and a bunch of stuff is happening and people do get decision fatigue and there is cognitive cost of all these things. But also there's an emotional aspect, which is, if your software stops me a second and asks me to make a decision and I don't really understand it, you make me feel stupid. I'm like, "I don't understand this." (00:37:50): Some people, maybe their orientation is, "Okay, the software is stupid." But I think most people are like, "Oh, I'm dumb." And if you ever talk to people who aren't especially technologically savvy, the canonical example is people who are under 50 talking to their parents about using some piece of software and what they're supposed to do, the parents always feel stupid like they're the ones that are wrong. And so if you're causing people to think, in the best case, it's unnecessary use of their biological resources, and in the worst case you've now made them feel bad, emotionally bad, and they're going to associate that with the product forever. And these are things that are just kind of rolling one into the other. (00:38:35): So I'm going to keep going with one last thing, because they just kind of come together, which is along with reduced friction, it's like reduce the number of clicks or taps it takes for someone to accomplish something which is almost always exactly the wrong thing. It's the easiest way you could make any action in your app, a single click or tap by just exposing every single possibility on one screen that scrolls for thousands and thousands and thousands and thousands of pages. And obviously that's terrible. So why do people think that a little bit of that is good? And here's an example. You open a menu, there's 14 things that people might want to do. (00:39:22): Level one is group them into like items and put a vertical, sorry, horizontal divider between them so at least people can kind of chunk and see what there is. Step two is present the two or three most common things or the five most common things, whatever and then have some form of other and then you go to a sub menu that has more items and the decision of how to tune that becomes incredibly important. I'm going to pick on Google again just because it is, I feel like I'm Donald Trump here, but I'm going to interrupt myself again with a story. It's-
turns.zh: 是啊。不过说实话，距离我上次读那本书已经过去十多年了，所以我甚至记不清书中所有例子了。但作为一个和效用曲线同等重要的法则，有两个原因。其一，决策本身代价高昂。你实实在在地消耗着葡萄糖。大脑活动会产生ATP，神经元也会激活一系列生理反应，人会产生决策疲劳，所有这些都需要耗费认知成本。其二，还有情感层面的影响。比如，如果软件突然让我做决定，而我又不明白怎么回事，那种感觉太糟糕了。我会想：“我根本不明白。”（00:37:50）有些人可能会想：“好吧，是软件太笨了。”但我觉得大多数人都会说：“哦，我真笨。”如果你和技术不太熟的人交流，典型的例子就是50岁以下的人和父母讨论使用某款软件时，父母总觉得自己错了，觉得自己很笨。所以即便你只是让用户思考，最好的情况下也是在浪费他们的生物资源；最坏的情况是让他们产生情绪上的负面体验，并且这种负面体验会永远和产品联系在一起。这些问题相互关联。（00:38:35）最后再说一点，因为这两者紧密相连——降低摩擦成本固然重要，但减少用户完成操作所需的点击次数往往适得其反。比如在应用里把所有可能的操作都堆积在一个滚动页面上，用户可能需要翻上千页才能找到正确的选项。这显然很糟糕。那么为什么人们觉得这样做有好处呢？举个例子。你打开一个菜单，里面有14个可能的操作选项。（00:39:22）第一步，把它们分成几组，用横线分隔开，让用户能快速分类和筛选。第二步，展示最常用的两三个选项，再加上其他选项的分类，最后再进入子菜单。这样用户的决策负担会大大减轻。我再拿谷歌举例——不是因为我想黑谷歌，而是因为我觉得自己像特朗普一样爱插嘴——我再讲个故事。谷歌的例子——

turns.en: Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好吧，说吧。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: At some conference or event, I don't remember what it was, and this is probably eight years ago and we're in the bar after the sessions ended at this thing. John Collison from Stripe is there and Sundar, CEO of Google is there. And John, sorry, Patrick goes up to Sundar and they can talk about anything. Stripe wasn't the behemoth, it was now at that point, but it was still a significant company, was up and coming. And what does Patrick want to talk to the Sundar about? It's in the Gmail app, the dragging of people. When you reply all to a message, you often want to change the two recipient to CC and move someone from CC to two or something like that. And just how physically the degree of dexterity that's required to do that inside of the Gmail app is very high. (00:40:56): It still hasn't been fixed, but it really struck me that Patrick could have asked for anything. It could have been any talk, it could have been a partnership. It was so irritating to him that it worked like this, he couldn't quite get over it. So anyway, back to bashing on Google, who in many respects do an incredible job and there's all kinds of amazing stuff they do on blah, blah, blah, but the Gmail actions on an individual email are broken into two very long menu items that are different. And one of them doesn't exist on either menu. There is an unlabeled icon is the only way to do it, and that's to mark something as unread once it's read. I have no idea why some of the actions are in one menu and some of the actions are in another menu. I think it's because some of them have to do with an individual email and some of them have to do with the whole thread, but it doesn't seem very consistent. (00:41:55): Every possible thing is listed there in one place. And so it becomes incredibly difficult to use because sometimes you have to tap in both menus, read all of the options, and say, "Okay, I've used the process of elimination and it's not here, so it must be there." Uber doesn't work like this anymore, but when I first brought this up to people inside of Slack, there was a moment when the Uber app, when you opened it was just, "Where would you like to go?" And other. And other was everything like change your payment method, set your location, anything you could do in Uber. And that was perfect because almost all the time people just wanted to choose where they wanted to go. Sometimes you wanted to change where your pickup was because you weren't there yet or whatever. And that was just like, what could be simpler than, "I'm going to tell you where I want to go or I'm going to achieve something else."? (00:42:47): I really tried to push people to what is the thing that people, or what is the two things or what is maybe three things that people could want to do here and then put everything behind other. And then if it takes them eight clicks or taps to do something, but every single one is trivially easy, that's great. If you reduce that to two clicks or taps, but every part of it is this fraught decision where I'm opening all of the menus and trying to figure out which thing is the right thing, and the more, comparing three things to each other is this difficult four things, it's kind of geometrically more expensive to compare 15 different options all to the other to see if this is the one that you might want. That just becomes impossibly expensive. So to me, those are all really connected. And if people could get over the idea of reducing friction as the [inaudible 00:43:42] or reducing the number of clicks or taps to do something and instead focus on how can I make this simple? How do I prevent people from having to think in order to use my software? How can I make this trivially easy? One last example, because this was really influential for me. So I was going back and forth in Vancouver in San Francisco at the time when we were talking about all this inside of Slack, and I was behind a teenager in line aboard the plane and it was like, we're on the jet way. It took a long time. And I was watching her use Snapchat and it was insane. (00:44:11): She was tapping at least four times a second, sometimes six or seven times a second. It was like dismissing stories and doing stuff. But there was a fluidity to it because everything was like, do I want to see this again? Do I want to see the next story from this person? Do I want to switch to a different person? Instead, a notification came up, she answered someone's thing, she took a selfie of herself and everything was just like... So she was tapping four times a second for six minutes. I mean, probably there was some breaks in there. And that was the highest and best use of Snapchat for a 15 year old girl in 2016 or whenever that was. And imagine if the goal was to try to make her tap less, how much of an impediment it would've been to the experience that both her and Snapchat wanted to create?
turns.zh:
在某次会议或活动上（我记不清具体是什么活动了，大概是八年前的事），我们在活动结束后去酒吧喝酒。Stripe公司的约翰·科里森（John Collison）和谷歌首席执行官桑达尔·皮查伊（Sundar Pichai）都在场。约翰（抱歉，应该是帕特里克·科里森）走上前去和桑达尔聊天，他们可以谈论任何话题。当时Stripe还不是巨头，但已经颇具规模，正在崛起。那么帕特里克想和桑达尔聊什么呢？是关于Gmail应用中拖动收件人功能的——当你给一封邮件回复所有收件人时，通常想把两位收件人改为抄送，或者把某人从抄送列表移到正文列表等操作。但在Gmail应用中实现这些操作所需的操作步骤实在繁琐。

（00:40:56）：这个问题至今仍未解决，但真正让我感到困扰的是，帕特里克本可以提出任何需求。原本可以是任何合作提案，但他对现有操作体验极度不满，难以释怀。说回谷歌，虽然谷歌在许多方面表现出色，有各种令人惊叹的功能，但Gmail应用中针对单封邮件的操作却被分散在两个冗长的菜单项中——其中一个菜单项甚至根本不存在。唯一的操作方式是点击未标注的图标，将已读邮件标记为未读。我完全不明白为何某些操作分散在不同菜单中。可能是部分操作针对单封邮件，部分针对整个邮件线程，但这种不一致性实在令人头疼。

（00:41:55）：所有可能的操作都集中在一个菜单项中。结果导致使用体验极差——有时你必须在两个菜单中逐项查找，尝试排除法，最终发现某个功能不在菜单里。Uber应用早就不这样了。但当我最初向Slack内部人员提出这个问题时，Uber应用刚推出时只有一个主界面：“你想去哪里？”其他选项包括更改支付方式、设置位置等所有功能。这才是理想的界面——用户几乎只想选择目的地，有时想更改接送地点等信息。操作步骤本可以更简单，比如“告诉我你想去哪里，或者选择其他功能”。

（00:42:47）：我试图向人们说明，用户可能希望在此处完成两件事（或三件事），然后将所有操作隐藏在其他菜单项下。如果操作步骤需要八次点击或轻触，但每个步骤都极其简单，那还好；但如果每个步骤都是痛苦的决策过程——不断打开菜单、比较不同选项——那就太糟糕了。比如比较15个不同选项之间的差异，简直是指数级复杂的任务。这实在令人难以承受。因此，在我看来，所有这些问题都是相互关联的。如果人们能摆脱“减少摩擦”或“减少操作步骤”的旧观念，转而专注于如何优化用户体验，那将是一个巨大的进步。
能把这事儿简单化吗？怎样才能让用户无需费脑子就能使用我的软件？如何做到操作极其简单？再举个例子吧，这个例子对我影响很深。当时我们在Slack上讨论这些问题时，我正来回穿梭于温哥华和旧金山两地。在飞机上排队时，我身后有个十几岁的女孩，当时我们正在滑行道上等候，过程很漫长。我看着她用Snapchat，简直太不可思议了（00:44:11）。她每秒至少点击四次，有时甚至六七次。整个过程流畅自然——比如，"我想再看一次这个？"、"想看这个人的下一条动态？"、"想切换到其他人？"——但每当有新通知弹出，她就回复别人，或者自拍一张，整个过程就顺其自然地继续下去。她连续六分钟每秒点击四次，中间可能偶尔停顿一下。这就是2016年那个15岁女孩对Snapchat的最佳使用方式。试想一下，如果目标是让用户减少操作次数，那对她和Snapchat想要打造的体验来说，会是多大的阻碍啊？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so fun to listen to this and the examples you gave of, it gives us a lot of insight into the way your mind works of just constantly unsatisfied with the way other products work with your product. And I think that's core. Patrick is a good example of Stripe. I feel like that's a recurring theme with very successful product leaders is just constantly unsatisfied and unhappy with how things work.
turns.zh: 听你讲这些例子真是太有趣了，这让我们深入了解了你的思维方式——你总是不满于其他产品与你们的产品的交互体验。我觉得这才是核心所在。帕特里克（Patrick）就是Stripe的典型例子。我觉得成功的产品负责人都有一个共同的特质，那就是对现有流程总是不满，总是不停地寻求改进。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just even the way you summarize this, just a really good reframing of, instead of obsessing with reducing friction and reducing steps, instead think, how do I reduce the amount of thinking the user has to do? I've never heard of it described as, you have to think about the ATP and glucose being used to actually think, and your goal is to reduce that versus let's just reduce friction, reduce clicks.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢你总结这个观点的方式，真是重新构思了一个思路——与其执着于减少摩擦、缩减步骤，不如思考如何减少用户的思考负担。我从未听过有人这样描述：你必须考虑ATP（腺苷三磷酸）和葡萄糖的消耗来进行思考，而你的目标应该是减少这些消耗，而不是简单地减少摩擦、减少点击次数。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. I think in my more cynical examples, I would say to people, " Stop what you're doing for a second, close-"
turns.zh: 是啊。我在更现实的例子中会对人们说：“先停下手中的工作，闭上眼睛——”

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Stop what you're doing for a second. Close your eyes, take a couple of deep breaths, and then pretend that you're an actual human being. And open their eyes again, and then look at this thing and see, can you figure out what it's supposed to do or say. Or what action you're supposed to take or what the impact will be if you take that action. There's a whole nother related cycle. But before I get into it, I know that I am verbose. I want to wrap up your last example of people being unsatisfied. (00:46:31): So here's the quote that I was trying to find. This is 2014, so like that was the year that Slack actually launched officially in February. And this is now near the end of the year. I was interviewed by MIT Technology Review and asked if we were working to improve Slack. I said, "Oh God, yeah. I try to instill this into the rest of the team, but certainly I feel like what we have right now is just a giant piece of shit. It's just terrible and we should be humiliated that we offer this to the public. Not everyone finds that motivational though." (00:47:06): So I came into the office the next day and people had printed out on like 40 pieces of 8.5 by 11 paper that quote, and pasted it up on the wall. But to me that was like, you should be embarrassed by it. It should be a perpetual desire to improve. You should probably be like, "Oh, this is great," and you could be proud of individual pieces of work. But in the aggregate, if you can't see almost limitless opportunities to improve, then you shouldn't be designing the product, or you shouldn't be in charge of the company, or you shouldn't almost nothing. (00:47:45): Again, you could reduce it down to a tiny feature is anywhere close to perfect. And if A, that's acknowledged freely inside the organization. And B, people think about continually improving as the goal. And that could be like Six Sigma Toyota, Kaizen, that kind of side of thing. Or it could be that story that... I can't remember his name right now. The guy who started Bridgewater tells about Michael Jordan-
turns.zh: 停下手中的工作，闭上眼睛，深呼吸几次，然后假装自己是个普通人。再睁开眼睛，审视眼前的事物，看看能否理解它的功能、提示用户该做什么，或者采取某个行动会产生什么影响。这背后还有一个完整的循环。但在深入探讨之前，我得承认自己话太多了。还是先回归到你最后提到的用户不满的例子吧。（00:46:31）：以下是我一直在找的那段引语。2014年，也就是Slack正式于2月推出的那一年。而现在已经接近年底了。我接受《麻省理工科技评论》的采访时，被问到我们是否在努力改进Slack。我回答：“天啊，是的。我试图把这种理念灌输给团队，但说实话，我觉得我们现在提供给公众的产品简直糟糕透顶。太烂了，我们应该为此感到羞愧。”（00:47:06）：第二天我到办公室时，人们把那段引语打印在40张8.5×11英寸的纸上，贴满了墙。但对我来说，这应该是一种耻辱。改进应该是永恒的追求。你或许会说：“这很棒”，为个别成果感到自豪。但从整体来看，如果你看不到几乎无限的改进机会，那你就不该负责产品设计，或是管理公司，几乎什么都做不了。（00:47:45）：再举个例子：如果你能把某个小功能做到近乎完美。A，公司内部要坦然承认这一点。B，人们要把持续改进视为目标。这可以是丰田的六西格玛、改善活动之类的思路，也可以是……我现在记不清他的名字了。桥水基金创始人讲的关于迈克尔·乔丹的故事——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ray Dalio.
turns.zh: 雷·达利奥。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, Ray Dalio in his book talks about Michael Jordan learning to ski. Every time he messed up, he wanted the ski instructor to tell him exactly what he was doing wrong. Because to him, every one of those was a gem that he could collect, and he could actually become a good skier. And what he wanted to do was become a good skier. That requires a lot of trust inside the organization. (00:48:36): But if you can get to the point where like, "Hey, we are trying to find improvements. We're trying to be critical because you're trying to make this as great as it can possibly be." And not always, not with every person, but most of the time with most people, you can get them to the point where that really direct criticism is actually motivational. It is like people are grateful to have the feedback, whether that's coming from their peers inside the company or from end users of the product. Because you realize, oh yeah, that is bad and we should fix it.
turns.zh: 是的，雷·达利奥在他的书中提到了迈克尔·乔丹学习滑雪的故事。每次他出错时，他都希望滑雪教练能准确指出他做错的地方。因为对他而言，每一次错误都是可以收集的宝贵经验，最终能让他成为一名优秀的滑雪者。他的目标就是成为一名出色的滑雪者。这需要组织内部高度的信任。（00:48:36）但如果你能让人们达成共识，比如：“嘿，我们正在努力寻找改进之处。我们试图保持批判性思维，因为我们想把事情做到尽可能完美。” 虽然这并非适用于所有人，但对大多数人来说，当你以这种方式提出批评时，它实际上会成为一种激励。无论是来自公司内部同事的反馈，还是产品最终用户的意见，人们都会心怀感激。因为他们会意识到，哦，对啊，这个问题确实存在，我们应该去改正它。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, so this is a lot to do with, and maybe this is more recently, it shows up in politics a lot for me. But by the way, if anyone listening to this can help me find this tweet store from somewhere between 2016 and 2020, I don't have a precise idea. And it was this guy's thread about how hard it was to get a stop sign set up. And I believe it was in response to someone claiming that Bitcoin is going to replace US dollars, something about crypto. And his point was like, here's what happened when we tried to get a stop sign put up on a residential street in my neighborhood. And the literal years it took, and the number of agencies that were involved. (00:50:58): Like the engineering department, traffic planners, the HOA, and... I don't remember all of the organizations because, and I did that I could search better and find this again. Because it was truly a masterpiece of how difficult it is to get a stop sign put up in most places. The message that I hear from most politicians, and unfortunately this works really well, is things should be good. But they're not because someone is doing something bad, which is preventing the goodness. (00:51:29): So billionaires are making things unaffordable. Or immigrants are taking your jobs. Or lazy freeloaders are sucking off a government tea, and causing us all have to pay more taxes, or something like that. The reality is almost nothing works. It's actually another call. I said in this case, John has a great encapsulation of this and I'm sure you're familiar with it, like that. It ends with the world as a museum of passion projects. Because for anything to get done at all requires not just the resources and effort required to instantiate that thing in the real world, but all of the politicking and the sociology and the convincing. (00:52:15): And there's a book called Why Nothing Works Recently, which is like, it's not an... I'm sorry to the author, if they... I doubt they're listening, but just it's not like an amazingly written book. I found it a little bit repetitive, but the content was really incredible, just explaining why it's so hard. And how there's this progressive increase in the number of vetoes that are available for any kind of course of action and how difficult it is... And this shows up in permitting for new construction and stuff like that. But also shows up obviously inside of organizations. (00:52:55): And the challenge is that people, A, I think this is evolutionary biological. It's hard for us to understand the world, except by anthropomorphizing it. And so if it didn't rain this year, it's because a God is mad, and probably because we didn't sacrifice enough goats or something last year. It's hard for people to understand just that, wow, weather is incredibly complex and chaotic, and ecosystems and climatology, and all that. (00:53:27): Same thing with the world. Like if I am struggling to pay all of my bills and be able to afford a little bit of luxury in the sense of location or a present for my kids or whatever, it's got to be somebody's fault. There has to be a decision that's made somewhere. And the reality is everything is so complicated. Everything is so multivariate, it's not satisfying. It's a terrible political message. (00:53:56): It's much easier to say that there is like, oh, we understand why things are bad in the way that you're concerned about. And it's turns out that it's some someone's decision, and because of them it's bad. And so if we got rid of them or were able to overcome their decision, overturn it, and institute our own thing, then things would be good for you. And this really to me shows up inside of those organizations as well. I'll pause there.
turns.zh:
是啊。我是说，这跟很多事情都有关，也许最近我在这方面在政治层面感受最深。不过顺便说一句，如果有听众能帮我找到2016年至2020年间某个推特帖子就太好了。我记得是关于在住宅区安装停车标志有多难的讨论。当时有人声称比特币会取代美元之类的，而他回应道：看看我们社区想在住宅区安装停车标志都费了多大劲。整个过程历时数年，涉及多个部门——工程部门、交通规划部门、业主协会等等（00:50:58）。我不记得所有机构名称了，因为我当时没能更好地搜索到那个帖子。但那确实是关于在大多数地方安装停车标志的难度的典型案例。我从大多数政客那里听到的信息（不幸的是这种说法很有效）是：事情本该美好，但因为有人作恶导致无法实现。比如亿万富翁让房价高不可攀，移民抢走工作，懒汉占便宜，政府开支导致税收增加之类的。但现实是几乎没有什么事情能真正奏效。这其实是另一个话题。我提到约翰对此有很棒的总结，我相信你们都熟悉那段话。最后他说世界成了激情项目的博物馆，因为要想真正做成一件事，不仅需要现实世界中的资源和努力，还需要各种政治博弈、社会协调和说服工作（00:52:15）。还有一本叫《为什么最近什么都行不通》的书，虽然作者写得不算惊艳（我觉得他可能不在听，但我还是要说），但内容确实很深刻，解释了为什么事情如此艰难。书中提到否决权的增加让任何行动都困难重重，这在新建项目审批等领域显而易见，也在组织内部普遍存在（00:52:55）。关键在于，人们要么认为这是进化生物学的结果——我们只能通过拟人化来理解世界。比如今年不下雨是因为上帝生气了，可能是因为去年我们祭祀的山羊不够多之类的。要让人们理解天气的复杂性和混乱，生态系统和气候学的复杂性实在太难了。（00:53:27）世界也是如此。比如当我难以支付账单，无法负担一点生活享受时，比如给孩子买礼物之类的，总得有人来背锅。问题是所有事情都太复杂了。变量太多，结果令人不满。这是糟糕的政治宣传。（00:53:56）更容易说的是：哦，我们理解你担心的那些糟糕状况。结果发现都是某人的决定导致的，只要我们摆脱他们或推翻他们的决定，建立自己的规则，一切就都好了。
这对你会很有好处。而这在我看来，在那些组织内部也同样适用。我先暂停一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know kind of along those lines, you're a big believer in something called Parkinson's Law.
turns.zh: 我大致明白你的意思，你对帕金森定律深信不疑。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. So the original of that is, I think it's 1956. It's an article in The Economist by Parkinson. And the Maxim is work expands to fill the time available for its completion. And the way that it shows up, this is a little bit subtle. So like one of the things I found, since I don't have a job is there's much less time pressure. And that maxim, like if you want something done, give it to a busy person. The inverse is also true that like, if you're not that busy, wow, basic things take a really long time. (00:55:09): And so Parkinson actually starts out with his example of writing and posting a letter. And I don't remember who he used with the first example, but someone who's incredibly busy and has all these things they have to respond to. And then another case like a retired robot who has all the time in the world. It takes her a long time to write the letter. It takes her a long time to put it in the envelope, and then you go to the post office and post it. (00:55:28): But the real meat of it is, for me later when he talks about the size of the organization, and he uses a bunch of examples. This is again 1950s, and he's British, so he's looking at the Royal Navy. And specifically he's looking at a chart that shows the relationship between the number of capital ships in the Navy, the number of sailors, and the number of administrators. And very familiar graph for people looking at any part of government. Any part of the relationship between the number of administrators at a university and the number of students and faculty, teaching faculty. Where it's like, okay, the number of ships goes like this and the number of sailors is looking right along with it. And the number of administrators goes like this. (00:56:14): And the reason this ties into the work expands to fill the time available for its completion is people hire, and they train. And here's the sad truth for anyone running a company is there are exceptions. There's certain types of engineers that are an exception to this. But the overwhelming majority of people you hire want to hire more people who report to them. And it's not because they're evil, and it's not because they're stupid. In fact, they're smart because everyone knows that the number of people who report to you correlates with your career trajectory, the amount of money that you're paid. The amount of authority you have inside the organization and on and on and on. (00:56:57): So we would hire 27 Royal product managers in Slack who immediately want to hire someone. It's like, what the hell? What would that person do? And they articulate it this way, but essentially it's like, "Well, that person would do the product management and then I would do strategy."
turns.zh: 是的。这个理论最初源于1956年。帕金森在《经济学人》上发表了一篇文章，核心观点是工作会不断膨胀，以填满可用的时间。这其中的逻辑比较微妙。比如，我发现自己失业后，时间压力就小了很多。帕金森提出的那个定律——“如果想让某件事完成，就把它交给一个忙碌的人。”反之亦然，如果你不那么忙，基本的事情反而会耗费大量时间。（00:55:09）帕金森举的例子是写信和邮寄信件。他用了两个案例：一个是超级忙碌、事务缠身的人；另一个是退休后闲得很的人。她写信要花很长时间，装信封也要很久，最后还要去邮局寄信。（00:55:28）但最有趣的部分是帕金森讲组织规模时，用了大量例子。那是1950年代的英国海军，他观察了舰船数量、船员数量和行政人员数量之间的关系。这对研究政府部门、大学师生比例等关系的人来说再熟悉不过了。舰船数量增加，船员数量随之增加，行政人员数量也相应增加。（00:56:14）帕金森指出，这个定律之所以成立，是因为人们会招聘和培训下属。对于企业管理者来说，最令人头疼的是存在例外情况。某些工程师可能不受此限，但绝大多数新员工都想招更多下属。这并非恶意或愚蠢，而是因为下属数量与个人职业晋升、薪资待遇、职权范围等息息相关。（00:56:57）比如我们Slack的27位皇家产品经理，一上来就想招人。我们问：“招来干什么？” 他们回答：“让他负责产品管理，我负责战略。”

turns.en: It's really, I think the essential thing to understand about this is it's not because people are evil, and it's not because they're stupid. And it's to me, very related to everything is complex. And if maybe this is my butterfly's law, I haven't thought about this way before. But I tweeted this a very, very long time ago like if you... Everything is simple if you have no idea what you're talking about. So the other side of that is like if something seems simple, probably you don't understand it. And there's obvious exceptions to that. (00:57:53): But for anything that involves a large organization or a lot of human beings, if the problem seems simple, you don't get it. So every budget process, no head of engineering know, head of sales, no CFO, no GC, who's ever going to come back and say, "Oh, I've actually think next year we can just hire fewer people. Or we're going to keep it flat or we're going to shrink through attrition because we don't need any more people to do what we're doing." Not because they're evil, not because they're stupid, but it's almost overpowering impulse inside the organization that often leads to disastrous results. And so there's an... (00:58:30): I'll give one example from Slack's history, and I have tried in the past to disguise this example so that no one feels bad about it but I... Unfortunately, the specifics are so important to the example that it's not disguised and so I'll just reiterate that the people involved aren't stupid or evil. And one example that's from the outside. So the example inside of Slack was we introduced threads, which was the ability to reply to a message inside of a channel. And let's say you, Lenny, post a message. I, Stewart reply to it. You will automatically get a notification. And now Sarah later on replies to the same message. Both you and I, as people who have push in that thread will receive a notification that there's been more activity, and so on. So like every single time anyone replies to it. (00:59:23): So when the feature first was released or like when we did the final product review before it was released, the input box was pre-populated with at the person before you in the thread. And I was using the feature and I would put the insertion point there, select all delete, and then start writing my message. And even if I wanted to add someone specifically, I almost never wanted to start my sentence with at that, because it just made it hard to reference what they were saying before. So I said, "Get rid of this because, A, I think most people won't use it. Or if they did want to add someone, they're not going to want to do it at the beginning of the sentence. (01:00:07): And by the way, you're teaching them to use the product wrong. Because it's important that everyone understand that every previous poster in this thread will automatically receive a notification unless they've figured it." (01:00:20): So okay, we release it. Six months goes by and suddenly the at thing comes back. And so I messaged someone around the team and I said, "Hey, there's been a regression. This is super weird. I don't know what happened. But the at thing came back." And they said, "Oh no, this is on purpose. We did a bunch of research." And so I was like, "What?" And I went through this and it was, if I recall correctly, it wasn't even P-95 certainty on this analysis. But it was something like when we do this, threads are 2.17 messages long, versus 2.14 messages long on average for when we don't do it. (01:00:59): And so first of all, why is a longer thread better? Like maybe a shorter thread is better? It can be fewer messages that people have to go back and forth. Also, that's such a tiny difference. Also, again, I don't remember the actual statistical analysis, so I'm not going to claim that it was incorrect. But I'm pretty sure this was outside the bounds of certainty that they can have. But the real thing was, oh my God, so you guys put flags into the product, you A-B tested it. You did the instrumentation. You created tables in the database or whatever we're using to record all of that. (01:01:39): You wrote queries to pull that. You created charts based on that data. You had meetings to discuss it. And just kind unpacking all of the things that would've had to happen for this to come back. And it's like thousands of person hours at a minimum, because any feature change at that scale of organization, it's involving like a dozen people. Engineering, QA, analytics teams, project managers, user research and stuff like that. The problem with that, so I think it was a bad idea, right? But the problem with that was the difference that you could possibly achieve between having this feature and not having this feature is like this much whatever units you want. The cost of doing the analysis was this much. So it's guaranteed to be a loser. (01:02:29): Like there's just, there's no world in which anyone could imagine putting the at previous respondent in the thread at the beginning of the message could possibly make that much of a difference to the quality of Slack, and how much utility it provides for people and all of that. But you know that to put the feature flags in, to ship new versions of the product, to put the instrumentation in. To have it all the API calls to record every action that people take to do all the analytics, to create the dashboard. To put paste a screenshot of that into a Google Slides presentation. To send the invitations to the meeting, to reschedule the meeting because someone couldn't make it. To have everyone sit down and look at the thing. Like guaranteed loser. (01:03:14): And I know that Fareed told you to ask me about this hyper realistic work-like activities. And so here's my grand theory. Hyper realistic work-like activities goes along with this other concept called known valuable work to do. And when I say known, I mean both you know what it is and you know that it's valuable. And the problem with almost every organization at the very beginning, you have an enormous amount of work that you know what to do, and you know that it's going to be valuable. So like starting a business, open a bank account. Because there's almost infinite general value of opening a bank account. You have to do it. It's very simple to do. (01:04:01): And so at the very beginning of any startup, they're like, "I'm creating a user's table, and I'm doing sorting passwords," and you're doing all the things that are kind of absolutely necessary. And everyone knows exactly what they are. And so everyone's going to work in the morning and they're like right on. And I have 10 things to do, and every single one of them is something I know how to do. And it's definitely going to be valuable. Time goes on. And the relationship between the supply of work to do and the demand for doing work just starts to change. (01:04:32): More and more people get hired. Every product manager wants to hire a junior product manager. Every new person, the first person you bring in on the risk and compliance team is like, "Oh my God, there's so many risks and things we have to be compliant with. We better hire more people on my team to do more risk and compliance work." Which probably to some degree is right. But we're going to have more and more of those people and they're going to call meetings with each other. (01:04:54): And now suddenly you have all these people with work to do and you've done all the easy obvious stuff. And now your questions are like, "God, should we do FedRAMP high and make a Slack version? Which is going to require us to have wholly separate physical infrastructure for the hardware that runs the software? And also a whole different operations team, which has only US citizens on it? What is the possible number of dollars that we could make from doing this? And how much complexity is going to be when we want to do updates to the software because we update two totally separate independent systems and rec." (01:05:27): It just gets out of whack, and so people end up... Like if you hire 17 product marketers, you're going to have 17 product marketers worth of demand for work to do. And if you don't have sufficient supply of product marketing work to do, they're just going to do other stuff. Again, very important, not because they're stupid, not because they're evil. But because they're like, I'm a product marketer and I want to be recognized for my work. And my spouse has criticized me because they take, I should have already got promoted in the last cycle, and they really got to demonstrate some wins here and whatever it is. (01:06:02): And so people are like calling meetings with their colleagues to preview the deck that they're going to show in the big meeting to get feedback on whether they should improve some of the slides. And that hyper-realistic work-like activity is superficially identical to work. Like we are sitting in a conference room and there's something being projected up there, and we're all talking about it. And that's exactly what work is. Hopefully not all of work for everyone inside of your company. But that's exactly what we do when we're working. (01:06:34): But this is actually a fake bit of work, and it's so subtle that I'll do it. Our board members will do it. Every executive will do it. And the further you are from having all of the context and all of the information and the decision-making authority and stuff like that, the easier it is to get trapped in this stuff. And people will just perform enormous amounts of hyper-realistic work-like activities, and have no idea that that's what they're doing. And the result of that, I guess, is that if you are a leader, if you're manager, director, an executive, you're the CEO, it's on you to ensure that there is sufficient supply of known valuable work to do. And there almost always is, but it's creating the clarity around that. Creating the alignment. Making sure everyone understands it, but that's what they're supposed to be doing, and then obviously doing it.

我认为，要理解这一点最关键的是，这既不是因为人们作恶，也不是因为他们愚蠢。在我看来，这与事物的复杂性息息相关。或许这就是我的蝴蝶效应定律——我以前从未这样想过。但很久以前我在推特上就说过：如果你……当你对自己所谈论的内容一无所知时，任何事情都会显得简单。反之，若某件事看似简单，往往意味着你根本不理解它。当然也有明显的例外情况。

（00:57:53）但对于任何涉及大型组织或众多人员的事务，若问题看似简单，往往意味着你没能理解全貌。例如，预算流程中，没有一位工程部主管、销售总监、首席财务官或总法律顾问会回头说：“哦，我觉得明年我们可以少招点人。或者保持规模不变，或者通过自然减员来缩减规模，因为我们不需要更多人来完成现有工作。”这不是因为他们作恶，也不是因为他们愚蠢，而是组织内部往往存在一种近乎压倒性的冲动，最终导致灾难性后果。因此，存在……（00:58:30）我将以Slack的历史为例。我曾试图淡化这个案例，以免让相关人员难堪，但……很遗憾，具体细节对案例至关重要，所以我还是要重申，相关人员既不愚蠢也不作恶。外部案例则是在Slack内部。我们推出了“线程”功能，即在频道内回复消息的功能。比如你（Lenny）发布一条消息，我（Stewart）回复你，你会自动收到通知。之后，Sarah再回复同一条消息。我们作为该线程的参与者都会收到有新动态的通知，如此循环。每次有人回复时，系统都会预先填入上一个回复者的用户名。我使用该功能时，会将光标置于用户名处，全选删除后再开始输入。即使我想特别添加某人，也几乎从不以用户名开头引用他们的内容。因此我说：“去掉这个功能，因为A，我觉得大多数人不会用它。即使有人想添加某人，也不会放在句首。”（01:00:07）顺便说一句，你这是在教他们错误使用产品。因为重要的是，所有参与者都要明白，除非他们已知晓，否则该线程中的所有前置回复者都会自动收到通知。（01:00:20）好吧，我们上线了这个功能。六个月后，“@”功能突然回归。我给团队成员发消息说：“嘿，出现回退了。这太奇怪了。我不知道发生了什么。但@功能又回来了。”他们说：“哦，不，这是故意的。我们做了大量研究。”我当时就说：“什么？” 我追问此事，如果我没记错的话，分析的置信度甚至不到95%。但数据显示，当我们启用该功能时，线程平均长度为2.17条消息，而未启用时平均长度为2.14条消息。（01:00:59）那么首先，线程更长更好吗？或许更短更好呢？
线程更好吗？这样用户就不用来回发消息了。不过这种差异实在微乎其微。再说一次，我不记得具体的统计分析了，所以我不会断言它有误。但我很确定这超出了他们能接受的置信度范围。但真正的问题是，天哪，你们居然在产品里加入了标志，还做了A/B测试，安装了监控工具，在数据库里创建表格来记录所有数据。（01:01:39）你们写了查询语句来提取数据，基于这些数据制作图表，开会讨论整个事宜。光是想想把这个功能上线所需的所有步骤，就得耗费数千个工时。因为在大型组织中，任何功能变更都需要十几个人参与——工程师、QA、分析团队、项目经理、用户研究等等。

问题在于，这个功能能带来的实际价值实在太有限了。而分析成本却高得离谱。所以这注定是个亏本买卖。（01:02:29）根本没人能想象，在消息开头加入“此前回复者已在此线程中回复”的标志，能对Slack的质量有多少提升，更别提为用户创造多大价值了。但光是添加功能标志、发布新版本、安装监控工具、追踪用户行为、创建仪表板、把截图插入Google Slides演示文稿、发送会议邀请、因他人缺席重新安排会议、组织大家开会讨论……这些步骤的成本简直难以估量。

我知道法里德让你来问我关于这些“超写实工作场景”的。这里我要提出一个大理论：超写实工作场景与“已知有价值的工作”这个概念息息相关。所谓“已知”，既指你清楚任务内容，也明白其价值所在。大多数组织在初期阶段，都面临着大量既明确又有价值的工作——比如创业公司开设银行账户。毕竟开户的通用价值近乎无限，你必须完成这个简单任务。

（01:03:14）初创公司刚起步时，大家忙着创建用户表、处理密码排序等基础工作。所有人都知道这些任务的必要性，也清楚其价值。早上上班时，每个人都信心满满：今天要做10件事，每项都是我擅长的，肯定能创造价值。但随着时间推移，工作供给与需求之间的平衡逐渐失衡。

（01:04:01）团队不断扩充，每个产品经理都想招个初级产品经理。风险合规团队新人入职时，第一句话往往是：“天哪，风险和合规条款太多了，我们得多招人。”
更多风险与合规工作。”这在某种程度上或许是对的。但我们将迎来越来越多这类人员，他们会互相召开会议。（01:04:54）：而现在突然间，所有这些人都有工作要做，而你已经完成了所有显而易见的简单任务。现在你的问题是，“天哪，我们是否应该采用FedRAMP高标准，并开发Slack版本？这将要求我们为运行软件的硬件配备完全独立的物理基础设施，还需要一个全美公民组成的运营团队？我们从中能赚多少钱？而当我们想更新软件时，又会面临多大的复杂性，因为我们要更新两个完全独立的系统。”（01:05:27）：这就会完全失控。因此人们最终会……比如，如果你雇佣了17位产品营销人员，你就会有17位产品营销人员需要完成的工作。若没有足够的产品营销工作供他们做，他们就会去做其他事情。再次强调，这很重要，不是因为他们愚蠢，也不是因为他们坏心眼。而是因为他们会想，“我是产品营销人员，我希望我的工作得到认可。”他们的配偶会批评他们，“你本该在上个晋升周期就升职了，现在你真的需要证明自己的价值。”（01:06:02）：所以人们会和同事开会预览他们要在大型会议上展示的PPT，征求反馈意见，决定是否需要改进某些幻灯片。这种高度逼真的工作活动表面上和实际工作一模一样。比如我们坐在会议室里，屏幕上投影着内容，大家都在讨论。这就是工作的样子。希望你公司里的每个人都不必如此。但这正是我们工作时会做的事情。（01:06:34）：但这实际上是一种虚假的工作，非常微妙，我也会做。我们的董事会成员会做。每位高管都会做。越是远离所有上下文、信息、决策权等资源的人，就越容易深陷其中。人们会进行大量高度逼真的工作活动，却不知道自己在做这些事。对此，我的看法是，如果你是领导者——无论是经理、总监、高管还是CEO——你的责任就是确保有足够的已知有价值的工作可做。这样的工作通常是存在的，但关键在于要清晰传达这一点，要达成共识，确保每个人都明白自己应该做什么，然后当然还要真正去行动。

If I had only exported all of my messages before I left, I would have all this stuff," but that was absolutely verbatim. I did not change a word of what I said inside the company.
