turns.zh: 嗯，那确实是一份内部备忘录，这里有点题外话。Slack的一个糟糕之处是，如果你所有的企业沟通都依赖邮件，取决于具体的系统和工作方式，你可能会留下在X公司说过的所有话的存档。如果是Slack，一旦你关闭账号，就无法访问这些历史记录了。所以就会想"天哪，如果我离开前导出所有消息就好了"，但内容完全一致。我在公司内部说的话一个字都没改。嗯，我们当时大概只有八个人。最多十个人，但我记得是八个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was before Slack launched even.
turns.zh: 那甚至是在Slack上线之前。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, it was before Slack launched. It was when we're doing private beta. And the point of it was to start to instill those ideas as early as possible and really create this alignment inside of that small team so that it could persist to survive as we grew and scaled. Yeah, that was the idea.
turns.zh: 对，是在Slack上线之前。当时我们还在做私有测试。目的是尽早开始灌输这些理念，在这个小团队中真正建立一致性，这样随着我们发展壮大，这些理念就能持续下去。是的，这就是初衷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the gist, just for people that aren't super familiar with it, but we'll link to it, is just it's not enough just to build a great product. You just as much have to put effort into communicating what this does for them, the problem this is solving for them, the outcome this is going to achieve for them. Is that a good way to think about it?
turns.zh: 关键点是（对于那些不太熟悉的人，我会附上链接）：光是开发出一个出色的产品是不够的。你还必须花心思去传达它能为用户解决什么问题、创造什么价值、带来什么成果。这是不是一个很好的思考方式？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. And again, comparing it to beer or cars, beer goes back to pre-civilization. Cars were obviously [inaudible 01:10:38], but at some point you had to convince people why they would want a car instead of a horse. For your new AI-based recruiting tool or your calendar app or whatever, there's some reason why you think that people should use yours instead of the thing that they're using now, which might be a wholesale one-for- one replacement, or more often is a change in the way that you're working that has a bunch of other adjacencies and you want to expand into these other categories. You're not just responsible for creating the product, but also, to a certain degree, creating the market. (01:11:15): There's this book, Positioning, which is an absolute classic. It's very short. I would recommend everyone read it, where the point of it is, from my perspective, it's almost impossible to create a new idea in someone's head. It's much easier to take a couple of existing ideas and put them together. So it's much easier to say it's like Jaws meets Star Wars, or it's Uber for Pets or something like that, than to come up with an actual new idea. But you have to do that because if your thing is different in any significant way from the alternatives, you're not just creating the product. You're creating the market. They're really kind of one and the same.
turns.zh: 是的。再举个例子，把啤酒和汽车作比较。啤酒的历史可以追溯到文明之前。汽车显然是（01:10:38，听不清），但在某个阶段，你必须说服人们为什么要选择汽车而不是马车。对于你的新AI招聘工具、日历应用或其他产品，你得给出一个理由，让人们相信应该用你的产品而非现有产品。这可能是一次彻底的替代，也可能是对现有工作方式的改进，从而开拓其他相关领域。你不仅要负责开发产品，还要在一定程度上开拓市场。（01:11:15）：有本经典著作叫《定位》，它非常简短。我推荐大家读一读。在我看来，要在人们脑中创造一个新概念几乎是不可能的。把几个已有的概念拼凑在一起要容易得多。所以比起想出一个全新的概念，比如“大白鲨遇上星球大战”，或者“宠物版优步”之类的，更容易的是把现有概念组合起来。但你必须这么做，因为如果你的产品与现有替代品有任何显著差异，你就不仅仅是在开发产品，还在开拓市场。两者其实是一体的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The reason I wanted to touch on it is I think still people continue to not listen to this advice and continue to over-invest in more features, more products, things like that. Just the specific example of, "We don't sell saddles here," just to quickly communicate this to folks, and correct me if I'm missing anything, is just instead of, "Hey, look at this amazing saddle we've bought," which you want to communicate as, "Here, go horseback riding. Look at this incredible experience you can have." And then they decide, "Oh, shit. I need to go buy a saddle to do that."
turns.zh: 我之所以想谈这个话题，是因为我发现很多人仍然不听从这种建议，继续在功能、产品等上过度投入。举个具体例子，“我们这里不卖马鞍”，快速跟大家解释一下（如果有遗漏请纠正）：你不应该强调“看，我们买了这个超棒的马鞍”，反而应该说：“来吧，去骑马吧。看看你能获得的绝佳体验。”然后他们会说：“哦，该死，我得去买个马鞍才能体验。”

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. And 100%, that aspect of it is not original because I think that's something that marketers have done for a long time, certainly in the marcom and advertising. If you want to sell Harley-Davidson's, there are people who are going to geek out on the engines and stuff like that and the quality of the leather and stuff like that. But when you're selling the motorcycle, you're selling the open road and freedom and the wind in your hair. And if you're Lululemon, you are obviously selling yoga pants, but you're also selling health and aspiration and being the best version of yourself and a bunch of other stuff. Oh my God, I forgot the classic version of it.
turns.zh: 是的。百分之百，这方面的思路并不新颖，因为营销人员长期以来一直这么做，尤其是在市场营销和广告领域。如果你想卖哈雷摩托，总有人会痴迷于引擎、皮革质量之类的东西。但当你卖摩托车时，你要传达的是开阔的道路、自由和迎风的感觉。如果是Lululemon，显然你卖的是瑜伽裤，但你同时也传递着健康、追求自我超越等价值观。天哪，我都忘了经典案例了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's the ship ...
turns.zh: 有一艘船……

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: You're selling the screwdriver.
turns.zh: 你卖的是螺丝刀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, yeah. The nail.
turns.zh: 哦，对。是钉子。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, the nail. Anyway.
turns.zh: 是的，钉子。总之。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we missed that one. Well, there's the one I think about is instead of trying to convince men to build a ship, instill a yearning for the sea.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们确实忽略了那一点。嗯，我想到的是——与其试图说服男人造船，不如激发他们对大海的向往。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yes. Exactly. That's something that goes back in history.
turns.zh: 对。没错。这件事在历史上由来已久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let me ask you about pivoting. You are potentially the king of pivots. You started two companies both famously pivoted, both from video games, which is why I asked you about that at the beginning, into very successful companies. I imagine many people come to you for advice on pivoting. Let me just ask when folks come to you asking, "Should I stick with my idea? Should I pivot?" what sort of advice do you find most helps them?
turns.zh: 好的。我想问问你关于转型的问题。你简直是转型之王。你创办过两家公司，都成功转型，而且都是从游戏领域起步的，这也是我一开始问你这个问题的原因。它们都发展得非常成功。我想很多人都会来找你寻求转型建议。让我问问，当人们来找你问“我应该坚持我的想法吗？还是应该转型？”时，你觉得什么样的建议对他们最有帮助？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think it's partly an intuition because obviously the decision is about, "Have you exhausted the possibilities?" and in the case where we were working on Glitch, this game where we used IRC for internal communication and we added a bunch of IRC which became the Proto Slack. I think Slack had an enormous advantage in the fact that we are working on this for several years without actually explicitly working on it and only doing the minimum number of features that were absolutely guaranteed to be successful in the sense that it was so irritating that we couldn't stand it anymore or such an obvious improvement that we couldn't help but take advantage of it. We still had $ 9 million left and everyone still liked the game and we were all happy working on it, but I think by that point I had exhausted every non-verdiculous long shot idea to make it commercially successful, and so I decided to abandon it. (01:14:52): But the default advice for anyone in anything is persevere. It's like a kitten hanging off the branch and a poster says, "Hang in there." There's so many stories of, "So-and-so started out going door-to-door and was rejected by everyone and then suddenly there was Nike," or something like that and just, "If you stick with it long enough, you'll eventually be successful." I think you have to really be coldly rational. Some of this shows up in the book Thinking in Bets. Some of it's in Annie Duke's second book, the title of which I'm forgetting right now, but someone will know it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这部分主要靠直觉，因为这个决定本质上就是在问：“你是否已经把所有可能性都用尽了？”就拿我们做Glitch这款游戏来说吧，当时我们用IRC做内部沟通，后来又加了很多IRC功能，最终演变成了Proto Slack。我认为Slack之所以能大获成功，主要在于我们花了好几年时间研发它，却没有明确以商业成功为目标，只开发了绝对能确保成功的功能。要么是用户忍无可忍，要么是优化得让人不得不改进。当时我们还有900万美元资金，用户也都喜欢这款游戏，大家都乐在其中，但我觉得那时我已经把所有非显而易见的长线可能性都探索完了，所以决定放弃它。（01:14:52）：但对于任何领域的人来说，默认建议都是坚持下去。这就像一只悬在树枝上的小猫，海报上写着“坚持下去”。有很多故事，比如某人开始挨家挨户推销，被所有人拒绝，然后突然就创立了耐克之类的。总之，“只要坚持足够久，最终就会成功。”我觉得你必须冷静理性。这些观点在《用数据思考》一书中有体现，安妮·杜克的第二本书里也有一些相关论述，不过我现在记不清书名了，但总有人记得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, Thinking in Bets, and then what was the second? I forget.
turns.zh: 对，《用数据思考》，那第二本是什么？我忘了。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: She actually uses Glitch and Slack as an example of a smart fold basically. My expected value here has diminished to the point where this alternative looks more attractive. And the reason I say you have to be coldly rational about it is because it's fucking humiliating. I convinced so many and you have to convince so many people to get a company off the ground. You have to go to investors. You have to go to early employees and say, "You should leave your other job and come work for this because here's the incredible feature we're imagining." You have to go to the press and you have to make all these promises and you have users and you've committed things to the users and you've convinced them to give up their time for this thing. And so I think for a lot of people, it feels better to just keep doing it until it dies of suffocation due to lack of capital or something like that. Then just to admit, "Okay, I was wrong. This didn't work," and it's humiliating. It's painful. It's wrenching. It has a bad impact. (01:16:46): When we shut down Glitch, there was a lot of people who loved it and would spend all of their free time and couldn't wait to get home from work to go play it more. And that was their community and the community just disappeared, all these people and all these identities that have been created. And obviously, people lost their jobs and people who had moved their families to a different city in order to take this job now weren't going to have a job anymore. So pivots aren't something I take lightly. I think it's very different to be like, "There's three of us and we started making this app and then we pivoted to a different app." That doesn't even really count. If you're six months into something, you're still messing around. You're trying to figure out what it is that you're building. It's not really a pivot. Obviously in this case, it worked out great and there's survivorship bias and that doesn't mean that everyone should pivot all the time. But I think creating the distance so that you can make an intellectual, rational decision about it rather than an emotional decision is essential.
turns.zh: 她实际上以 Glitch 和 Slack 为例，说明了所谓的"聪明折腾"。我预期的收益已经低到这种程度，以至于这种替代方案看起来更具吸引力。我之所以说你必须冷静理性地看待这件事，是因为这他妈的太丢脸了。我说服了那么多人，而要让一家公司起步，你又得说服更多人。你得去找投资者，找早期员工，说："你应该辞掉现在的工作来为我们工作，因为我们构想了一个不可思议的功能。"你还得面对媒体，许下种种承诺，用户们信任了你，让他们为此投入时间。然后，当资本短缺或其他问题导致公司倒闭时，你不得不承认："好吧，我错了。这玩意儿不行了。"这太丢脸了。这很痛苦。这让人心碎。这会产生负面影响。（01:16:46）：当我们关闭 Glitch 时，很多用户都非常喜欢它，他们会利用所有空闲时间玩这款游戏，迫不及待下班回家继续玩。这就是他们的社区，而这个社区就这样消失了，所有这些人和创建的所有身份都没了。显然，人们失去了工作，那些为了这份工作搬到新城市的人也将失业。所以转型不是我能轻易对待的。我认为像"我们三个人开始开发这个应用，然后转型到另一个应用"这种情况根本不算转型。如果你已经做了六个月，还在摸索阶段，那根本不算转型。显然这次转型很成功，但这只是幸存者偏差，并不意味着每个人都应该一直转型。但我认为保持距离至关重要，这样你才能做出理性的、基于逻辑的决策，而不是情绪化的决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love, also, your piece of advice of just exhaust. Once you've exhausted all the ideas, that's a really good time to see what else is out there.
turns.zh: 我也喜欢你提到的彻底尝试的建议。一旦你用尽了所有想法，那就是看看还有什么其他可能性的好时机。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, just all the good ideas.
turns.zh: 是的，所有好的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All the good ideas,
turns.zh: 所有好的想法，

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: All the realistic. Yeah.
turns.zh: 所有现实的想法。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The point you made about just kind of persevering, I just had Melanie Perkins, CEO of Canva, in the podcast. 100 investors rejected her before somebody finally decided to invest and she just kept pushing.
turns.zh: 是的。你提到的坚持不懈的观点，我最近在播客上采访了 Canva 的首席执行官梅兰妮·珀金斯。在被 100 位投资者拒绝后，终于有人决定投资，她就一直坚持下去。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's a slightly different example, right? She eventually believed in the concept of the product and in the vision. It was just trying to figure out the right articulation to get investors who ended up being obviously very, very happy.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得这是一个稍微不同的例子，对吧？她最终相信了产品的概念和愿景。只是在想办法用合适的表达方式说服投资者，而投资者最终显然非常满意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely happy. Oh, geez. Okay. Maybe a final topic depending on how time goes. I want to talk about generosity. I talked to a bunch of people, as I said, that have worked with you and the number one theme that came up again and again and again when I asked them about you and what has stuck most with them is just generosity. So I'm going to read a few examples that I heard from folks that are examples of your generosity over the years. (01:18:57): So one person shared that he needed a little money before Christmas and he said, "Stewart literally walked me out of the building, went to the cash machine, handed me $500, told me to go home to my family." Other folks shared that, when you talked about Glitch just recently when you had to lay people off, you cried real tears when you were laying people off and then you spent an incredible amount of time helping them find new jobs and extending their severance pay and just taking it extremely, extremely seriously, much more than I think most people feel like CEOs do. Someone else shared that you paid 100% of employees health insurance to give them just fewer things to think about. (01:19:35): When you went public, you basically created the best possible situation for employees, no lockup, direct listing. Also, with the structure of the Slack deal, people said that acquisition was very employee friendly. That's employees. There's also just the way you thought about customers. A few examples: You gave free credits to businesses who were struggling to pay the bills during COVID. You released this fair billing, which I think was very innovative at the time, where you stopped charging people for seats they weren't using, even though they signed a deal to charge for those seats. A lot of times, you slipped release schedules because you just wanted to make features better and better for people. And I'll end with this quote: "Stewart is a leader who takes the responsibility he feels for his employees personally, and to which he extends the most generous circumstances he could muster. That feels worth celebrating." (01:20:25): So first of all, I just want to celebrate you. I think it's really rare and inspiring to meet a leader like that. Clearly, you've had a lot of impact on a lot of people. I don't know exactly the question I want to ask, but I guess in what part is this intentional, just like, "This is how we win. I'm going to be very generous and help people because I know this will help long-term"? How much of this is just a [inaudible 01:20:48] and it's just the way you are as a person?
turns.zh:
非常开心。天哪。好吧。或许最后再探讨一个话题，看看时间如何安排。我想谈谈慷慨之心。我和很多与你共事过的人聊过，正如我之前所说，当我问起你时，他们反复提及的一个主题就是你的慷慨。所以我要分享几个例子，都是我从人们那里听来的，展现了你多年来的慷慨之举。（01:18:57）：比如，有人分享说圣诞节前他急需一笔钱，“斯图尔特直接带我走出大楼，取出500美元递给我，让我回家与家人团聚”。其他人则讲述，当你最近谈及裁员时，面对离职员工，你流下了真诚的泪水，随后花费大量时间帮助他们寻找新工作、延长离职补偿金，展现出远超多数人对CEO所期待的关怀程度。还有人提到，你为员工全额支付健康保险，让他们无需为琐事操心。（01:19:35）：上市时，你为员工创造了最佳条件——无需禁售期，直接上市。Slack交易的结构也被称赞为对员工极为友好。再说你对客户的考量：新冠疫情期间，为支付账单困难的企业免费提供信用额度；推出公平计费模式——当时这在业界堪称创新之举，停止向未使用座位收费；多次延期发布功能，只为让产品体验更出色。最后引用一段评价："斯图尔特是一位将对员工的责任感视为个人使命，并竭尽全力为他们创造最优环境的领袖。这份胸怀值得赞颂。"
（01:20:25）：首先，我想为你喝彩。能遇到这样的领袖实属难得且振奋人心。显然，你对许多人产生了深远影响。我不确定具体想问什么，但我想探讨其中有多少是刻意为之——比如"这就是我们的胜利之道，我要慷慨相助，因为我深知这对长远有益"？又有多少只是你骨子里的善良？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: I think a lot of it is just the way I am as a person and I had wonderful parents who raised me right, but I think there is a little bit of a lesson there and I'm just going to assume people's familiarity with the prisoner's dilemma. The acts of generosity to me are, "Oh, I am demonstrating that I am going to cooperate as we iterate in this game." And if you do that, then people will also cooperate and you both benefit. Whereas if you never really know if the other person is going to defect at the first opportunity, then your best bet is to defect. And so there's a game theoretic aspect, usually in games that are much, much, much more complicated than the prisoner's dilemma. (01:21:36): I think one thing I didn't touch on before, but to me was important enough, is that at more than one company all hands, I made everyone in the company repeat this as a chant. It was, "In the long run, the measure of our success will be the amount of value that we create for customers." And I wanted to be super clear and explicit about that because it should be if anything you're doing feels like a little bit shady, a little bit cheating, a little bit maximizing at the wrong moment or taking advantage of a customer or anything like that, definitely shouldn't do it. Because to me, I mean I think it's literally true, but it's also an ethical way to run a business. And it's not just that the ethics are good. It's like there's advantages for you. You're able to attract a better class of employees. If all your employees are ethical, then it's going to be a better place for everyone to work and you're going to be happier and you're going to have fewer internal problems and all that stuff. (01:22:48): But I think it really is true that especially in the long run, you can't destroy value for your customers and expect to be successful. You have to actually make their lives better. And you could put effort into pointing it out to them and demonstrating that you have created this value and stuff like that, but there's no substitute for actually having created it. And I think that is incredibly important and that implies a real generosity, whether that's in negotiating terms with an enterprise deal or that's policy decisions. One time that it blew up in our face was our SLA was like, "For any downtime, you get 100 times your money back." Because from my perspective, it's like if we're down for two minutes, it's like pennies. It doesn't really make any difference. If we're down for 10 hours or something like that, then we have bigger problems than paying back people. (01:23:51): Fast-forward, we now have hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue and we've gone public. And shortly after we go public, we have one of the biggest outages we ever had. I don't remember how long it was, but it was many hours. But by the time we got that scale, 100 times the money back for the third of a day that we were down was $8 million or something like that. It didn't cost us any money because we just gave it to people in the form of credits, but it meant that a bunch of revenue that we had already anticipated for the next quarter wasn't going to show up because people's credits were going to offset what they would've otherwise paid us. And so we definitely changed the terms of service after that because being a public company is a little bit different. But in every other respect, I think they were all really important decisions that were helpful in us becoming successful.
turns.zh:
我认为这很大程度上取决于我的个人性格——我有幸得到父母的正确教养，但这背后也有一些值得反思的道理。我假设大家都熟悉"囚徒困境"这个博弈理论。对我来说，慷慨之举往往意味着："在博弈过程中，通过合作来证明自己的诚意"。若你能做到这一点，别人也会配合，最终实现双赢。但若你永远不确定对方是否会第一时间背叛，那么最佳策略就是选择背叛。因此，博弈论的思维方式在许多比囚徒困境复杂得多的场景中都适用。

（01:21:36）：还有一点我之前没提到，但对我来说很重要——在多家公司，我曾让全体员工将这句话当作口号反复宣扬："从长远来看，我们成功的衡量标准是为客户创造的价值。" 我之所以强调这一点，是因为如果你做任何事时感到有些不道德、作弊、在错误时机追求利益最大化、利用客户等等，那绝对不该这么做。对我而言，这不仅是字面意义上的正确，也是经营企业的伦理准则。伦理不仅有益，更能带来实实在在的好处：吸引更优秀的员工队伍。若全体员工都秉持道德准则，工作环境必将更加和谐，员工更快乐，内部问题更少。

（01:22:48）：但从长远来看，确实不能以损害客户利益为代价换取成功。你必须真正为他们创造价值。可以努力向他们指出并证明你创造了价值，但唯有实际创造的价值才最有说服力。无论是在企业协议谈判中还是政策制定上，这种慷慨都至关重要。曾有一次我们吃了苦头——我们的服务级别协议写着"停机时赔偿100倍服务费"。但在我看来，两分钟停机损失微不足道，而10小时停机带来的损失远超赔偿金额。

（01:23:51）：快进到现在，我们营收已达数亿美元，成功上市。但上市后不久，我们遭遇了史上最大规模的停机事故，持续数小时。我不记得具体时长，但按当时规模计算，停机半天赔偿8百万美元。但我们以积分形式补偿用户，实际未产生任何成本。但这意味着原本预期的下一季度营收被抵消，因为用户积分会抵扣应付款项。因此上市后我们调整了服务条款，毕竟上市公司运营方式有所不同。但除此之外，我认为所有决策都对我们的成功起到了重要推动作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was that policy ... It was automatic? You didn't even have to claim it. It was just automatically you get this credit?
turns.zh: 那个政策……它是自动的吗？你甚至都不需要主动申请。只要符合条件，就会自动为你发放这笔补偿金？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: And the default is you don't have to pay if you let us know. This was, "We will automatically, proactively, preemptively without any input from you ..."
turns.zh: 而且默认设置是，如果你告知我们，就无需付费。这句话是：“我们会自动、主动、先发制人地为你处理……”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Too generous.
turns.zh: 太慷慨了。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: "Apply this credit to your account, and just send you a message that it happened. And by the way, we will do it on the aggregate for downtime, even if the issue didn't affect you as a customer."
turns.zh: “将这笔补偿金存入你的账户，然后给你发个通知说已经处理了。顺便说一下，即使故障没有影响到你作为客户，我们也会统一处理所有停机时间的补偿。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Too generous. You found the edge of where you want to be.
turns.zh: 哇。太慷慨了。你找到了理想的平衡点。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was that mantra again that you had the company chant? I think this is a really nice way to end it.
turns.zh: 你之前让公司念的那句口号是什么来着？我觉得用这个来结束整个对话真是再合适不过了。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: It was, "In the long run, the measure of our success will be the amount of value we create for customers."
turns.zh: 是“从长远来看，我们成功的衡量标准将是为客户创造的价值。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible. I'm just trying to picture the entire team at Slack reciting this mantra.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。我现在就在想象整个Slack团队念这句话的情景。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: It was hundreds of people. It felt very like, Kim Jong-Un or Stalin or something like that.
turns.zh: 有几百人呢。那种感觉就像金正恩、斯大林之类的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, on that note, most people don't know this about you, but your actual name when you were born was not Stewart. It was Dharma.
turns.zh: 好吧，说到这儿，大多数人都不知道这件事，但你出生时的真名不是Stewart，而是Dharma。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this all makes sense as you learn that.
turns.zh: 现在回想起来，一切都说得通了。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. My name is Dharma Jeremy Butterfield, so my parents named me. And when I was 12, I changed it because I just really wanted to be normal and for some reason I thought Stewart was a normal name. And by the way, you'll notice this now that I said it. Any character except for Stuart Little the mouse, anytime you see a character in a movie, a novel, TV show or whatever, there's only the loser Stewart and the asshole Stewart. It's obviously, in the collective consciousness, a terrible name and I shouldn't have chosen it and I regret it. But by the time I realized that, Dharma and Greg had already come out and it would've seemed like I was bandwagon jumping. And people thought it was a girl's name, even though in India it's obviously only a boy's name. (01:26:32): I'm going to add just one last little tidbit because I forgot about this earlier on and I think it helps tie things together, and it's called the owner's delusion. And this is based on something I posted on Twitter. The person who came up with the name later deleted their account and so I have no idea who it was and who to credit for this. But what I had posted was, and this was a long time ago when restaurant websites have gotten better and it doesn't really matter because Google Local was taking over everything, but this is, let's say, 10 years ago. (01:27:00): There's five things you could possibly want when you go to a restaurant's website and it's their street address, their phone number, the menu, the hours of operation ... Oh my God, I'm forgetting the fifth thing. Oh, and making a reservation, how to make a reservation. And again, this problem has to some extent taken care of it's itself or at least improved, but what you would get was this super slow loading photo, the Ken Burns effect as it [inaudible 01:27:30] ...
turns.zh: 是的。我叫Dharma Jeremy Butterfield，是父母给我起的名字。12岁那年，我改了名字，因为当时特别想正常一点，不知为何觉得Stewart是个正常名字。顺便说一句，现在你应该能注意到，我说了这事儿。除了《小鼠奇兵》里的Stewart之外，任何角色只要出现在电影、小说、电视剧里的，要么是失败者Stewart，要么是混蛋Stewart。在大众意识里，这显然是个糟糕的名字，我不该选它，现在很后悔。但等我意识到这一点时，《达尔马与格雷格》已经播出了，我要是换个名字就会显得跟风了。还有人以为这是女孩名，尽管在印度显然只有男孩才叫Dharma。（01:26:32）：最后再补充一个小细节，我之前忘了说的，但我觉得能把整个故事串起来。这叫“所有者错觉”。这是基于我在Twitter上发过的一篇帖子。后来那个取名的人删掉了账号，所以不知道是谁，但还是要感谢他。当时我发的是关于餐厅网站的，现在已经改善了很多，但当时（10年前吧）情况很糟糕。（01:27:00）：去餐厅网站可能希望了解的五件事：地址、电话、菜单、营业时间……哦，第五个我忘了。对了，还有预订功能。现在这个问题在一定程度上已经解决了，或者至少有所改进，但当时你得到的只是一张加载超慢的照片，肯·伯恩斯效果……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The flashed.
turns.zh: 它闪了一下。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: And then fading in and then some music starts playing. And then if they show you the phone number, it's not clickable.
turns.zh: 然后逐渐显现，随后音乐响起。如果他们给你显示电话号码，那还不能点击。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Image.
turns.zh: 图片。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: It's not even text that you can copy because yes, it's an image. And they don't have the hours. They don't put the address or whatever and it's just like, "What?" For sure, whoever made this website for the restaurant owner and the restaurant owner themselves have definitely been in the position where they went to somebody else's restaurant website because they wanted to get the address or the opening hours or the phone number or whatever. So why does it end up like this and what should we call this? (01:28:01): And whoever replied to the tweet, she said, "We should call it the owner's delusion," and I was like, "Oh my God. That's perfect." And I think that is incredibly powerful and what ends up with the result, like Apple naming whatever that feature is called Sleep, which it's too hard to understand what that can possibly mean. And that's why people anticipate, despite the fact that when they get to your website for the first time, their intent is absolutely the minimum number of micro points above the threshold required from them to actually take that action. (01:28:41): You're like, "All right. Welcome to my website," and there's a bunch of BS and there's a bunch of stuff that doesn't make any sense and the buttons are inscrutable. And it's unclear what to do next because I think that my thing is so important and I don't recognize that you are at work and you were late this morning and you have to go to the bathroom and you're just a regular human being who has stuff going on, that you're concerned that your kid is a fuck-up and they're getting in trouble at school and stuff like that. They're not subjects who paid money to go to your play and are sitting in the audience and waiting for that curtain to go out. They're people who are going to bounce in a fraction of a second. And so everyone should always be conscious of the owner's solution.
turns.zh: 甚至都不是可以复制的文本，因为没错，那是个图片。他们没有标注营业时间、地址之类的，就只是个问号。毫无疑问，无论是为餐厅老板制作这个网站的人，还是老板本人，在访问别人餐厅的网站时，肯定都曾遇到过这样的困境——他们想获取地址、营业时间、电话号码之类的，却发现页面设计糟糕透顶。那么为什么会这样呢？我们该怎么称呼这种情况？（01:28:01）：回复这条推文的人说，"我们应该称之为老板的妄想症"，我当时就想，"天哪，太贴切了。"我觉得这句话非常有力，能总结出最终的结果。比如苹果给Sleep功能起的名字，太难理解了。这就是为什么人们会预期，即便他们第一次访问你的网站，动机也是最基本的——完成某个操作所需的最低门槛。但结果往往令人失望。比如你说"欢迎来到我的网站"，然后一堆废话、莫名其妙的内容，按钮更是让人摸不着头脑。用户不清楚下一步该做什么，因为你可能觉得自己的事务很重要，却忽略了用户可能在工作、迟到、需要上厕所，或者正为孩子在学校惹麻烦而焦虑。他们可不是花钱来看你的戏剧、坐在观众席等待幕布升起的观众。他们是随时会离开的普通用户。所以每个网站设计者都应该时刻留意用户的真实需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. What's the solution? Is it have other people look at it and give you feedback?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种分析。解决方案是什么？让其他人看看并给出反馈吗？

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah, and recognize it. And unfortunately, it's one of those things like Murphy's Law.
turns.zh: 是的，并意识到这一点。不幸的是，这就像墨菲定律一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Even you can go wrong even when you take into account Murphy's Law.
turns.zh: 即使考虑到墨菲定律，也可能出错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: But if you don't name it and recognize it and discuss it and train yourself to think that way, take a breath, pretend you're a regular person, and then look at this again and see if it makes sense, then you're screwed.
turns.zh: 但如果你不给它命名、识别它、讨论它、训练自己以这种思维方式，深呼吸，假装自己是普通人，再重新审视是否合理，那你就完蛋了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I love that you threw this in here. I have a billion other questions I'm going to ask you in part two when we do this someday. Stewart, thank you so much for doing this. Thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你提到的这些见解。我还有无数其他问题想在下次访谈中问你，等哪天有机会再说。斯图尔特，非常感谢你参与这次访谈。感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Stewart Butterfield
turns.en: Yeah. Thank you for having me, Lenny. I really enjoyed it.
turns.zh: 是啊。感谢邀请，莱尼。我真的很享受这次交流。
